target.title: fix(browser): cap fields-file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Browser CLI action commands accept `--fields-file` for form field descriptors. The previous reader loaded the whole file into memory before validating or parsing it, so a very large fields file could be fully buffered before the CLI rejected it.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a narrow 1 MiB byte cap to the `--fields-file` path only. The reader consumes at most the cap plus one sentinel byte, rejects oversized files before JSON parsing, documents the limit in Browser CLI help and docs, and leaves inline `--fields` behavior unchanged.

## User Impact

Users get a friendly size-limit error for oversized Browser CLI fields files instead of the CLI buffering arbitrarily large input. Existing valid fields files up to the documented 1 MiB limit and inline JSON fields continue to work.

## Evidence

Current head: `e029080cbc7f9ff23196914e772a6959a739b480`.

- Real behavior proof: `node --import ./node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs --input-type=module <inline proof script>` imported `readFields` from the current head and exercised valid, exact-limit, and oversized `--fields-file` inputs while confirming the Browser CLI docs mention the 1 MiB contract. Final terminal output:

```json
{
  "head": "e029080cbc7f9ff23196914e772a6959a739b480",
  "maxBytes": 1048576,
  "validFieldsFile": [
    {
      "ref": "proof-ref",
      "type": "text",
      "value": "from file"
    }
  ],
  "exactLimitFieldsFile": {
    "bytes": 1048576,
    "ref": "exact-ref",
    "valueLength": 1048544
  },
  "oversizedFieldsFile": {
    "accepted": false,
    "error": "fields file exceeds 1048576 bytes"
  },
  "docsMentionLimit": true
}
```

- Focused test: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/register.form-wait-eval.test.ts` passed 2 files / 19 tests.
- Formatting and whitespace: `node_modules\.bin\oxfmt.CMD --check docs/cli/browser.md extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/register.form-wait-eval.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.ts` passed; `git diff --check origin/qingminlong/browser-fields-file-cap-v2~1...HEAD -- docs/cli/browser.md extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/register.form-wait-eval.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.ts` passed.

target.title: feat(gateway): pre-handshake WS verifyClient with Sec-Fetch-Site and forwarded-header hardening
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's gateway already validates browser `Origin` on the WebSocket path, but only **post-handshake** (in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-admission.ts`, after the socket is already open), and it does **not** defend against:

- **Header-smuggling / contradiction attacks** — a client forging `X-Forwarded-For` to disagree with `Forwarded` (or vice-versa) to confuse the resolved client IP / trust decision.
- **Cross-site WebSocket initiations (CSRF / DNS-rebinding class)** — there is no `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate anywhere in `main` (`git grep` confirms zero `sec-fetch-site` enforcement in `src/`).
- **Proto contradiction** — `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `Forwarded proto` disagreeing with the actual socket transport (without breaking legitimate TLS-terminating trusted proxies).

These gaps are the WebSocket sibling of the HTTP ingress CSRF findings **#102834** (addressed on main) and **#96486**, and sit *under* the origin-allowlist work in **#98924** (which decides *which* origins pass, not *when/how the gate runs*).

This PR adds a self-contained **pre-handshake** `verifyClient` gate attached to the gateway `WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })`, so unauthenticated or forged clients never complete the HTTP 101 upgrade.

The WebSocket upgrade phase is the only reliable point where the forwarded-header, proto-mismatch, and `Sec-Fetch-Site` signals are available for enforcement. Once the handshake completes, post-handshake WebSocket admission logic no longer has access to them.

**Distinct from adjacent items:** #102881 (merged) closed the HTTP `auth.mode=none` CSRF gap by adding `checkBrowserOrigin` to the HTTP auth path, post-routing. This PR is the WebSocket-upgrade sibling — it adds a pre-handshake `verifyClient` so header-only signals (forged forwarded headers, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, proto mismatch) can be rejected before the 101, on a surface #102881 does not touch. The existing post-handshake origin check in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-admission.ts` remains unchanged and authoritative for role-scoped decisions (`isBrowserOperatorUi` / `isWebchat` / `isNativeAppUi`).

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Pre-handshake beats post-handshake.** Running the checks in `verifyClient` (before the 101) means a rejected client never gets a live socket, matching the defense-in-depth posture maintainers expect for a network-exposed gateway.
- **Reuses the shared `checkBrowserOrigin`** rather than reinventing origin logic, so allowlist / same-host / loopback behavior stays consistent with the HTTP/WS admission paths.
- **All strictness is opt-in and default-off** (`gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation`, `rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders`, `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests`), so existing deployments have **zero behavior change**. Non-browser clients (CLI, native apps) send no `Origin` and pass through; they authenticate post-handshake as today.
- **Trusted proxies are correctly exempted** from the proto-mismatch check — a TLS-terminating proxy legitimately presents plaintext to the gateway.

This is complementary to **#98924** (`allowedOriginPatterns`): that PR extends *which* loopback origins are allowed; this PR adds the *enforcement layer* (pre-handshake gate, header contradiction, `Sec-Fetch-Site`). Neither duplicates the other.

## Prior Attempt & What Improved

This is a follow-up to my earlier (closed) PR **#35109** (`fix(gateway): surgical proxy-aware origin validation`), which edited the shared `checkBrowserOrigin` on the *post-handshake* WS path. Compared to that attempt, this PR:

- Moves the gate to **pre-handshake** (`verifyClient` before the 101) instead of extending the post-handshake check — a rejected client never opens a socket.
- Adds the **`Sec-Fetch-Site` cross-site rejection** and **`X-Forwarded-For` vs `Forwarded` IP-contradiction** checks that #35109 did not cover.
- Keeps the change **self-contained** in `verify-client.ts` + `forwarded-headers.ts` rather than widening the shared `checkBrowserOrigin` contract used by every HTTP/WS caller.
- Ran the `autoreview` closeout gate before opening; it caught a real **`Origin: null` bypass** (a literal `null` origin was treated like an absent header and skipped all browser validation). Fixed in `verify-client.ts` with a regression test — the gate now only fast-passes on a *truly absent* Origin.

The goal was to take the earlier direction, make it architecturally cleaner, and actually vet it before asking for review.

## User Impact

- Network-exposed gateways gain a pre-handshake defense against forged forwarded headers and cross-site WebSocket CSRF, with **no config change required** for existing users (all new behavior opt-in).
- Operators who want stricter posture can enable:
  - `gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation` — reject duplicate / comma-chained sensitive proxy headers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders` — reject proxy headers from non-trusted peers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` — reject `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` / `cross-origin` WebSocket upgrades. **Off by default**; opt in only when every legitimate browser WS client is same-origin to the gateway. Loopback aliases (e.g. `localhost` -> `127.0.0.1`) are legitimately flagged cross-site by browsers, so the gate stays opt-in and `checkBrowserOrigin` remains authoritative.

## Evidence

### End-to-end verification using a real `ws.WebSocketServer` and the production `createGatewayVerifyClient` path (head `1b5c1de`)

A real `node:http` server was bound on `127.0.0.1:18901` with a real
`ws.WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, verifyClient })`, wired through the actual
`createGatewayVerifyClient` from `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts`. Real HTTP
Upgrade requests were sent with browser/proxy headers and the observed status
line was recorded. This is not a mock — the wire path is the same path the
production gateway uses. Scenarios below were chosen to cover every case
ClawSweeper's prior review listed (browser, proxy, loopback-alias, native-client,
IPv4, IPv6).

```
== 1. native client (no Origin, no proxy headers) — non-browser pass-through ==
   request headers: {"host":"127.0.0.1:18901"}
   observed: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  ->  ACCEPTED

== 2. loopback-alias browser Origin (localhost -> 127.0.0.1, cross-site) ==
   [regression guard for v2026.4.15 / PR #66665 shipped contract]
   request headers: {"origin":"http://localhost:5173","host":"127.0.0.1:18901","sec-fetch-site":"cross-site"}
   observed: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  ->  ACCEPTED

== 3. allowed browser Origin (allowlist match) ==
   request headers: {"origin":"https://app.example.com","host":"127.0.0.1:18901"}
   observed: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  ->  ACCEPTED

== 4. disallowed browser Origin (not in allowlist) ==
   request headers: {"origin":"https://evil.example.com","host":"127.0.0.1:18901"}
   [verify-client] origin not allowed (origin not allowed)
   observed: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden  ->  REJECTED
   body: origin not allowed

== 5. cross-site WS rejection (Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site) with flag OPT-IN ==
   config gateway.security: {"rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests":true}
   request headers: {"origin":"https://app.example.com","host":"127.0.0.1:18901","sec-fetch-site":"cross-site"}
   [verify-client] cross-site websocket request rejected (sec-fetch-site=cross-site)
   observed: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden  ->  REJECTED
   body: cross-site request rejected

== 6. forwarded-header contradiction (X-Forwarded-For vs Forwarded, IPv6) ==
   [proves canonical IPv6 parsing — fixes split(":")[0] truncation finding]
   request headers: {"origin":"https://app.example.com","x-forwarded-for":"2001:db8::1","forwarded":"for=\"[2001:db8::dead:beef]\""}
   [verify-client] forwarded header inconsistency: X-Forwarded-For resolves to 2001:db8::1 but Forwarded resolves to 2001:db8::dead:beef
   observed: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  ->  REJECTED
   body: invalid headers

== 7. forwarded-header AGREEMENT (matching IPv6 across forms: bracketed+port vs bracketed) ==
   [proves bracketed-with-port normalizes to bracketed IPv6; would have failed under old parser]
   request headers: {"x-forwarded-for":"[2001:db8::1]:12345","forwarded":"for=\"[2001:db8::1]\""}
   observed: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  ->  ACCEPTED

== 8. proto mismatch from UNTRUSTED peer (X-Forwarded-Proto: https on plaintext) ==
   request headers: {"x-forwarded-proto":"https"}  trustedProxies=[]
   [verify-client] origin protocol (http) does not match X-Forwarded-Proto (https)
   observed: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  ->  REJECTED
   body: invalid protocol

== 9. proto mismatch from TRUSTED proxy (legitimate TLS-terminating proxy) ==
   request headers: {"x-forwarded-proto":"https","x-forwarded-host":"app.example.com"}  trustedProxies=[127.0.0.1/32]
   observed: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  ->  ACCEPTED

== 10. untrusted proxy headers (rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders opt-in) ==
   config gateway.security: {"rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders":true}  trustedProxies=[]
   request headers: {"x-forwarded-for":"203.0.113.7"}
   [verify-client] proxy headers from untrusted address (remote=127.0.0.1)
   observed: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden  ->  REJECTED
   body: proxy headers from untrusted source

== 11. literal 'null' browser Origin (opaque context) does not bypass the gate ==
   request headers: {"origin":"null"}
   [verify-client] origin not allowed (origin missing or invalid)
   observed: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden  ->  REJECTED
   body: origin not allowed

SUMMARY: 11/11 scenarios observed at the expected HTTP status code.
```

### Focused tests and gates on head `1b5c1de`

- `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` — **8/8 passing** (trusted-proxy wiring regression, untrusted-peer reject, cross-site reject when opted in, **loopback cross-site allow by default** (v2026.4.15 regression guard), `Origin: null` reject, non-browser pass-through, IPv6 contradiction, IPv6 matching-across-forms).
- `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` — **22/22 passing** (config-contract parity for new `gateway.security.*` fields).
- `tsgo` core typecheck: **clean (exit 0)**.
- `oxlint` on touched files: **0 warnings, 0 errors**.
- `oxfmt --check` on touched files: **clean**.
- `autoreview` (Codex, high reasoning): initially reported the `Origin: null` bypass; after the fix, no accepted/actionable findings.

## Scope / Out of scope

- **In scope:** `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts` (new, wired at `server-runtime-state.ts`), `src/gateway/forwarded-headers.ts` (validators), their tests, and the `gateway.security.*` config surface in `src/config/types.gateway.ts` + `src/config/zod-schema.ts`.
- **Out of scope (left to maintainer decision):** the `#98924` allowlist-wildcard contract, and the broader `gateway.browserOrigins` client/role-scoped policy direction.
- **`Sec-Fetch-Site` note for reviewers:** upstream deliberately avoids a blanket `cross-site` reject on MCP **HTTP** because browsers flag legit local MCP as cross-site. This PR mirrors that posture for the **WebSocket upgrade** path: the reject is **opt-in** (`gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests: true`) and runs *after* `checkBrowserOrigin`, so the existing origin allowlist / loopback-alias admission (shipped in v2026.4.15, PR #66665) remains authoritative. Native/CLI clients send no `Sec-Fetch-Site` header so they pass through regardless.

## Related

- Sibling enforcement: **#98924** (`allowedOriginPatterns`, open) — which origins are allowed.
- Prior art (security findings this complements, addressed on main by earlier work): **#102834** (HTTP ingress CSRF under `auth.mode=none`), **#96486** (CSRF via the existing `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`, which this PR reuses verbatim rather than duplicating).
- Prior attempt by me: **#35109** (closed) — see "Prior Attempt & What Improved".

cc @steipete — this sits on the gateway origin/security boundary you own (and is the sibling of #98924 / #102834 and #96486, both addressed on main by earlier work). The `Sec-Fetch-Site` reject is scoped to the WS upgrade pre-handshake specifically because of the MCP-HTTP caveat you handled; happy to align flag names / gate position with #98924 before merge if you'd prefer.


---

## ClawSweeper Follow-up (head `1b5c1de`)

Addressed all four findings from the July 17 ClawSweeper review in a single follow-up commit (`1b5c1de7ed5`):

1. **[P1] Default-on Sec-Fetch-Site reject → opt-in.** `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` now defaults to `false` (`=== true` instead of `!== false`), matching this PR's stated "all flags default-off" design and preserving the v2026.4.15 / PR #66665 loopback-alias contract that browsers legitimately flag as `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`. Regression test added (`allows legitimate loopback cross-site traffic by default`).
2. **[P1] Duplicate config field removed.** `gateway.security.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback` is gone; `verify-client` now reads the existing `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback` so pre-handshake and post-handshake admission share one source of truth.
3. **[P2] Canonical IPv6 parsing.** `forwarded-headers.ts` now uses `normalizeIpAddress` from `@openclaw/net-policy/ip` instead of `split(":")[0]`. Bracketed / unbracketed / port-suffixed IPv6 literals all normalize correctly. Regression tests added for IPv6 contradiction detection and matching-across-forms.
4. **[P2] Public config contract completed.** `gateway.security` plus its three leaf fields now have entries in `schema.labels.ts`, `schema.tags.ts`, and `schema.help.ts` (all ≥80 chars with operational guidance, per `schema.help.quality.test.ts`).

Net diff: +50/-40 prod LOC across 8 files. The PR got smaller, not larger. All unit tests (`verify-client`: 8/8, `schema.help.quality`: 22/22) and `tsgo` core typecheck are green on the new head.

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)

## What Problem This Solves

`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` in `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.ts`
uses the same exponential backoff schedule (`500ms / 1000ms / 2000ms`) for ALL retryable
embedding errors — including provider rate-limit (429 / quota-exhausted) errors. Rate-limit
windows are typically 60s; the short backoff burns all retry attempts within 2 seconds while
the window is still active, causing the entire memory index operation to fail.

The issue log shows 8 retries all landing within the same second:
```
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 583ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 589ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 519ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 588ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1032ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1024ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1058ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1170ms
```

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adds `isRateLimitMemoryEmbeddingError()` to detect 429/rate-limit/quota-exhaustion
errors specifically, and extends `runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop()` with optional
`rateLimitBaseDelayMs` / `rateLimitMaxDelayMs` params. When a rate-limit error is detected,
the retry switches from the standard transport schedule to a longer schedule (10s/20s/40s,
capped at 60s) that clears the provider's cooldown window.

## User Impact

Memory indexing (`openclaw memory index`) against rate-limited embedding providers
(e.g. Google Gemini free tier, AWS Bedrock with low TPM quotas) now survives transient
rate-limit windows instead of failing after exhausting all retries within 2 seconds.

## Evidence

### Real gateway verification (Windows, ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct)

Gateway startup log confirms memory-core extension loads from the updated dist and
all 13 plugins initialize without errors:

```
[gateway] loading configuration…
[gateway] resolving authentication…
[gateway] starting...
[plugins] loading memory-core from D:\openclaw\dist\extensions\memory-core\index.js
Registered plugin command: /dreaming (plugin: memory-core)
...
[plugins] loaded 13 plugin(s) (13 attempted) in 128.7ms
[gateway] agent model: ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct (thinking=off, fast=off)
[gateway] http server listening (13 plugins: …, memory-core, ollama, …; 4.7s)
[gateway] ready
```

Gateway Control UI responds correctly:
```
GET http://127.0.0.1:18789/ → 200 OK (text/html, 15376 bytes)
GET http://127.0.0.1:18789/v1/status → 200 OK
```

### Vitest

```
$ npx vitest run extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  19 passed (19)
   Start at  15:33:49
   Duration  475ms
```

### Backoff comparison

| Error type | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Transient (ECONNRESET, socket hang up) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s | **unchanged** |
| Rate limit (429, quota exhausted) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s | **10s / 20s / 40s** (capped 60s) |

### Not tested

- Live 429 rate-limit scenario against a real rate-limited provider (ollama is local
  and does not enforce rate limits; the retry-backoff schedule is verified via unit
  tests that simulate 429 errors with measured delay assertions)
- `postJsonWithRetry` in `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-http.ts` — that is a
  separate, lower-level HTTP retry layer (3 attempts, 300ms–2000ms); the embedding
  manager retry loop in this PR operates one level above and catches errors from the
  entire batch operation including timeout and provider-level errors

target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): guard provider isConfigured probe against malformed config throws
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveConfiguredCapabilityProvider` calls the `isProviderConfigured` callback without try/catch. The callback is a direct passthrough to the provider's own `isConfigured` — if that throws (e.g. Gradium on a malformed `baseUrl`), the exception crashes capability resolution. This affects realtime transcription provider selection in voice-call and TTS provider talk routing.

This is the third sibling of #108569 (Gradium provider fix) and #110506 (TTs persona resolution fix) — all three fix the same throw-in-isConfigured pattern at different call sites.

## Fix

Wrap the callback invocation in try/catch. A thrown exception returns `{ ok: false, code: "provider-not-configured" }` — the same result as a provider that reports unconfigured — so other providers remain selectable.

## Evidence

### Before fix

A realtime transcription provider with a broken `isConfigured`:

## What Problem This Solves

`resolvePrimaryTtsProviderCandidate` calls `provider.isConfigured()` without try/catch protection. target.title: fix(baseten): reject malformed model metadata numbers

## What Problem This Solves

Baseten live model discovery trusted JavaScript-only numeric string forms from `/models` metadata. Malformed strings such as hexadecimal limits, `NaN`, or prices that overflow after per-million scaling could override curated context-window, max-token, or pricing metadata instead of falling back to the bundled catalog values.

## Why This Change Was Made

Invalid live values are ignored so bundled fallback metadata remains authoritative for malformed rows.

## User Impact

Baseten model catalogs no longer surface inflated or malformed live context windows, token limits, or per-token prices, while valid decimal/exponent live metadata can continue to update bundled catalog values.

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit; no concurrent store open or migration can enter that unrecorded window.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Evidence

- 27 focused PortGuardian store/spawn and RemotePortTunnel tests pass, including concurrent writers, exact compare-delete, PID reuse, live process reconciliation, mixed-version capability checks, peer migration, receipt retry, reservation exclusion, and exact-child cleanup.
- 20 adjacent PortGuardian planner/process tests pass, including a real orphaned tunnel process.
- 5 shared native SQLite bootstrap/transaction tests pass.
- Node state-schema adoption: 85 passed, 1 skipped; database-first guard suite: 489 passed.
- macOS `OpenClaw` product build passes with Xcode beta.
- SwiftFormat, strict SwiftLint, `git diff --check`, database-first legacy-store guard, package-script syntax, and plist validation pass.
- Fresh autoreview and independent runtime/CDHash review report no actionable residual findings.

AI assistance was used for implementation and review. Maintainer-directed design, focused tests, and exact-head validation were performed locally.

target.title: fix(signal): preserve reverse-proxy path prefixes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running the native Signal channel behind a reverse proxy path prefix, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8080/signal`, would still send RPC, health-check, and SSE requests to the origin root (`/api/v1/...`) instead of the configured prefix (`/signal/api/v1/...`).

That can make Signal send/check/receive flows fail with 404s even though `channels.signal.httpUrl` points at the correct mounted Signal service.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveSignalEndpointUrl` now keeps the parsed base URL pathname before appending the Signal native endpoint suffix. Root-mounted base URLs keep the existing `/api/v1/...` behavior, while path-prefixed base URLs now resolve beneath the configured prefix.

The change is limited to the native Signal client URL join helper. Container-mode Signal URL construction is separate and already preserves its configured path prefix, so it is intentionally unchanged.

## User Impact

Operators can run the native Signal HTTP/SSE API behind a path-prefixed reverse proxy and use the same configured `httpUrl` for sends, health checks, and event streaming.

## Evidence

target.title: perf(ui): drop typebox from Control UI startup by lazy-loading the approval page
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI initial loads carry more JavaScript than the page needs: every boot downloads and evaluates the full typebox runtime (schema builders, value checks, format validators, and its locale tables) even though only the standalone `/approve` document page uses it. That inflates cold loads, updates (new hashed assets), and remote/Tailscale sessions where the startup payload dominates time-to-interactive.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follow-up to #110472. Startup-bundle attribution through the build sourcemaps showed typebox as the single largest startup module group (130 KiB raw), reachable only via `app-host.ts`'s static import of the approval page registration — the one page not behind a lazy route. The approval page imports `approval-result-validators`, which compiles protocol schemas with typebox at module init.

The fix uses the repo's existing `OptionalCustomElement` seam (already used for the terminal panel, browser panel, and command palette): `openclaw-approval-page` now registers through a lazy module load, preloaded only when bootstrap resolves an approval document mode from the URL. The approval document template already renders a booting splash as light-DOM fallback, so the load gap is covered by design. Startup budgets are ratcheted to the new baseline (340 KiB gzip, 20 requests) per the budget script's "budget changes accompany an intentional loading decision" contract, so the win cannot silently erode.

## User Impact

Every Control UI load ships 47 KiB gzip (~250 KiB raw) less JavaScript and makes 9 fewer startup requests: startup JS drops from 369.1 KiB gzip / 22 requests to 321.8 KiB / 13 requests (−13%). Cold loads, post-update loads, and slow links benefit most. The `/approve` approval flow is unchanged: the page lazy-loads on approval URLs and renders identically.

## Evidence

- Startup attribution (sourcemap byte accounting across startup chunks): typebox 130.4 KiB raw was the largest npm group, present only via the approval-page chain; `frame-guards` and the other boot-reachable protocol modules are type-only imports and stay startup-safe.
- `node scripts/check-control-ui-performance.mjs`: startup JS 321.8 KiB gzip / 13 requests (was 369.1 KiB / 22 on main); all budgets green including the new tighter limits.
- Live verification on a real-data dev gateway: `/approve/<id>` lazy-defines and renders the approval page (correct "Approval unavailable" state for an unknown id); normal chat boot renders with no approval module in the network log.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/e2e/approval-page.e2e.test.ts` — 6 e2e tests drive a real browser against the built UI at `/approve` and pass through the lazy path.
- Focused units: `ui/src/app` (273 tests), `approval-page.test.ts` (12), `test/scripts/control-ui-performance.test.ts` — all pass.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two sidebar-footer nits:

1. The warning-severity "Model auth expiring: <provider> (...)" attention chip nags for OAuth tokens that roll expiry continuously (e.g. short-lived tokens), creating recurring noise for auth that still works.
2. The lobster pet and the brand logo coexist without interacting: ledge visits never touch the logo, so the only playful logo moment is the rare perch load.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The expiring chip is removed; the error-severity "Model auth expired" chip stays, so genuinely broken auth still surfaces with a route to Model Providers.
- Ledge visits now sometimes scare the logo away: a seeded 30% roll per arrival, a ~900ms beat after the crab settles in, the logo fades out via the existing `sidebar-brand__logo--vacated` transition (no stand-in renders), and the existing `presence -> out` edge restores it when the visit ends. Perch visits, offline summons, and `prefers-reduced-motion` users are exempt. The existing `LOBSTER_LOGO_VISIT_EVENT` channel is reused with a lookless detail variant, so the sidebar needs no new event surface.

## User Impact

- No more recurring "auth expiring" warnings; expired/missing auth still alerts.
- Roughly a third of idle lobster visits now play a small "crab scared the logo" gag; the logo always returns when the visit ends. Reduced-motion users see no change.

## Evidence

Before (crab visiting, logo present bottom-left) / after (logo scared away, crab stays):

| Before | Scare |
| --- | --- |
| ![before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/logo-scare-2026-07/logo-before.png) | ![scare](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/logo-scare-2026-07/logo-scare.png) |

## What Problem This Solves

`loadBootFile` in `src/gateway/boot.ts` read the workspace `BOOT.md` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, allowing an arbitrarily large file to be loaded into memory during gateway boot.

target.title: fix(googlechat): journal webhook events before ack
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Google Chat webhook acks inbound events with HTTP 200 **before** dispatching them. `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-webhook.ts:353-363` fires `void runDetachedWebhookWork(() => params.processEvent(...))` and immediately answers `res.statusCode = 200; res.end("{}")`. There is no journal anywhere on the path — `monitor-routing.ts` wires `processEvent` straight to dispatch.

A gateway crash (or restart, OOM, deploy) in the window between the 200 and the detached dispatch permanently loses the user message: Google Chat treats the 200 as final delivery and does not retry webhooks. A dispatch failure is only logged (`runtime.error`), never recovered. The user sees their message vanish with no error on either side.

## Why This Change Was Made

This mirrors the maintainer-blessed inbound-durability wave already landed for sibling channels: sms #109866 (Twilio webhook spool), msteams #110357 (journal before webhook ack), discord #110274, whatsapp #110418, imessage #110409, mattermost #110386. Google Chat was the remaining webhook channel with the ack-then-lose window.

Mechanism, owner boundary, and storage follow the sms spool shape exactly:

- **Journal before ack** (`monitor-webhook.ts`): after auth + parse, `MESSAGE` events are admitted through `target.ingress.enqueue(event)` — a durable append to the existing shared-state `channel_ingress_events` queue (`runtime.state.openChannelIngressQueue`, same seam sms/msteams/discord already use; **no schema change**). Only after SQLite commits does the webhook answer 200. An enqueue failure propagates to the plugin HTTP route layer, which answers 500 — a honest non-ack instead of a false one.
- **Dedupe key** = the Google Chat message resource name (`spaces/<space>/messages/<message>`, the platform uniqueness contract), lane = space name, matching msteams' `event_id = activity.id, lane = conversation.id`.
- **Drain + replay** (`monitor-ingress.ts`, new): `createGoogleChatIngressSpool` wraps `createChannelIngressDrain` with retry/dead-letter classification and 24h/20k completed + 30d/1k failed tombstones (sms values). The owning monitor (`monitor.ts`) drains on a 500ms interval and once at startup, so events journaled before a crash replay after restart; entries are tombstoned only after turn adoption via `bindIngressLifecycleToReplyOptions` wired into `core.channel.inbound.run({ turnAdoptionLifecycle })`.
- **Journal boundary**: `CARD_CLICKED` approval clicks and space lifecycle events run dedicated non-agent workflows and keep the existing detached path — the same twin-check boundary msteams #110357 used (messageUpdate/votes/consent excluded). No SDK/core changes; everything lives in the googlechat plugin.

## User Impact

- A gateway crash or restart no longer loses Google Chat user messages that were already acked: they replay from the durable queue on startup.
- Redelivered duplicates (same `message.name`) are acked without dispatching twice, via completed tombstones.
- If durable admission itself fails (e.g. state DB unavailable), Google gets a 500 instead of a false 200, so the failure is visible instead of silent.
- No config, schema, or API changes; CARD_CLICKED approval flow unchanged.

## Evidence

### Loss window (before fix, `origin/main` @ `00eb33fe8e`)

`monitor-webhook.ts:351-363`: detached `runDetachedWebhookWork(processEvent)` + immediate `res.statusCode = 200; res.end("{}")`. Reverse verification: with the prod fix reverted (`git checkout HEAD -- monitor-webhook.ts monitor.ts monitor-types.ts`), the new durability test goes red exactly at the durability assertion:

```
FAIL extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.webhook-durability.test.ts
  × replays a 200-acked message after a restart that killed dispatch
AssertionError: expected [] to deeply equal [ ObjectContaining{…} ]
  - Expected: [ { id: "spaces/AAA/messages/durable-1", laneKey: "space:spaces/AAA" } ]
  + Received: []        ← 200 already sent, nothing journaled: message lost on restart
```

### Real-behavior proof (after fix)

`monitor.webhook-durability.test.ts` drives the **real webhook handler** through a real loopback HTTP server (`withServer` from `plugin-sdk/test-env`) with the real body reader, rate/in-flight limiters, and a real SQLite ingress queue in a temp state dir:

1. `POST /googlechat` with a `MESSAGE` event → **200 `{}`** (auth stubbed via `vi.mock("./auth.js")`, the only mock; admission path is fully real).
2. Assert dispatch never ran and the event **is durable**: `listPending()` returns `{ id: "spaces/AAA/messages/durable-1", laneKey: "space:spaces/AAA" }`.
3. Simulate crash: `spool.dispose()` with no drain.
4. Fresh spool over the same state dir (restart) → `drainOnce()` → dispatch called **exactly once** with the journaled event payload intact (`message.text: "are you there?"`, user, eventTime preserved).
5. Second restart → tombstone holds, **no second dispatch**.

`monitor-ingress.test.ts` (real SQLite queue, no mocks) additionally proves: pending-event recovery across instances, **claimed-mid-dispatch reclaim** after owner death (the crash-between-claim-and-adopt window), completed-tombstone dedupe (`kind: "completed", duplicate: true` on re-enqueue, single dispatch), space-based lane key, and refusal to journal a `MESSAGE` event without `message.name`.

### Test suite

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-ingress.test.ts \
    extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.webhook-durability.test.ts \
    extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-webhook.test.ts \
    extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.webhook-routing.test.ts \
    extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.test.ts
Test Files  5 passed (5)

```

target.title: feat(linux): native gateway transport for Quick Chat — device identity, TLS pinning, ack-driven sends
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Linux Quick Chat (#110285) sends by spawning the CLI per message: no delivery acks, a fresh process per send, agent identity via a CLI field instead of the gateway's own contract, and no connectivity awareness. This PR gives the Linux app a real native gateway connection — the same trust class the macOS app has — and routes Quick Chat through it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three gateway security contracts shaped the design, each verified in source before building (none were relaxed):

1. Browser-origin token-only sockets get their scopes cleared by design (`connect-auth.ts`), so a webview WebSocket client was rejected.
2. A native client id alone does not grant operator scopes either — device-less shared-token auth collapses `operator.read` to `[]` (proven by the existing `server.auth.default-token.suite.ts`). The macOS app's real trust class is a persistent device identity with nonce-bound challenge signing.
3. Self-signed gateway TLS (`gateway.tls.autoGenerate`) cannot be verified by system roots, and mDNS fingerprints are not an authoritative trust source.

What ships, accordingly:

- **Native WebSocket client** (`gateway_ws.rs`, tokio-tungstenite): connect/hello handshake, request/response correlation with timeouts, `agents.list` + `chat.send` with ack classification, 1–30s capped reconnect backoff, heartbeat watchdog. Auth material never reaches the webview; the invoke API surface for `quickchat.js` is unchanged in shape.
- **Persistent device identity** (`gateway_device_identity.rs`, ed25519-dalek): Ed25519 keypair + endpoint-bound reusable device token, atomic 0600 storage in the app config dir, zeroized credential buffers, v3 nonce-bound signature byte-identical to the macOS/OpenClawKit layout (fixture-bytes test).
- **Auth surface (flagged for maintainer review)**: additive `openclaw-linux` entry in the closed client-id set; the native-app UI predicate extracted to one shared helper (`isNativeAppUiClient`) that admission now uses, with Linux added alongside macOS/iOS/Android; new dedicated test file proving direct-local pairing auto-approves and remote pairing stays explicit.
- **TLS trust handoff**: `dashboard --json` additively emits the gateway's authoritative leaf-cert SHA-256 (same canonical format as `src/infra/tls/fingerprint.ts` and the discovery `gatewayTlsSha256` field) only when TLS is enabled; the Rust connector pins it with a constant-time compare (custom rustls verifier that still enforces handshake-signature validity), uses system roots when no pin is handed off, and rejects a pin on plain `ws://`. Trust failures surface distinctly from downtime.
- **Quick Chat integration**: identity/agents/switcher served from the gateway list (render-ready `identity.avatarUrl`), sends via `chat.send` with UUID idempotency keys and macOS-identical routing (global scope ⇒ `global` + agentId), a connectivity strip driven by connection-state events, and the entire CLI spawn path (`spawn_agent_turn`, message temp files, CLI list structs) deleted.

Known limitations, deliberate: SecretRef-configured tokens are withheld from the handoff (already-paired installs keep working via device token; first-run documented), ack-only send classification (terminal turn outcome stays in the session), streamed replies are the named follow-up.

## User Impact

Linux Quick Chat sends now get real accepted/failed acks from the gateway, agent identities and avatars come straight from the gateway contract, a slim strip shows when the gateway is unreachable (with automatic reconnect), and the app pairs itself as a first-class local device — visible and manageable like the macOS app. Docs updated (`docs/platforms/linux.md`).

## Evidence

Live end-to-end in an Ubuntu 24.04 container running a real repo-built gateway (token auth, three seeded agents):

| Paired + gateway-served avatar | Message staged |
| --- | --- |
| ![bar](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-bar.png) | ![typed](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-typed.png) |

| Gateway killed → strip | Gateway restarted → auto-recovery |
| --- | --- |
| ![strip](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-strip2.png) | ![recovered](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-recovered.png) |

The live run exercised the full new path: dashboard handoff (`wsUrl` + fragment token) → connect/hello → device pairing (direct-local auto-approve; `quickchat-gateway-device.json` persisted mode 0600) → `agents.list` with avatar → send → gateway kill → "Gateway unreachable — retrying" → restart → reconnect via reused device token.

Validation:

- `cargo +1.93 fmt --check` and `cargo test --locked`: 69/69 (Blacksmith Testbox run 29633282403, and re-verified in the Linux container on the final head).
- Focused Vitest across every touched TS surface: 43/43, plus the relocated Linux admission test (33/33 in the shared suite unchanged).
- `pnpm build` clean in the container; `node --check` on the JS; `git diff --check` clean.
- Dependency health checks recorded for `tokio-tungstenite` 0.30.0, `ed25519-dalek` 3.0.0, `rustls` 0.23.42, `subtle` 2.6.1.
- Structured second-model review: multiple rounds during the build (accepted findings fixed); the final round's two P1 deserialization claims were verified false against source — both structs carry `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` (`gateway.rs:104`, `gateway_ws.rs:188`) — and are additionally disproven by the live container run above, which decodes both payloads on that exact code.

target.title: fix(ui): prevent appended chat rows from overlapping
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Control UI transcript rows stacking on top of each other when a new message is appended after a tall reply, including image-paste turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

#110472 made the thread and row Lit refs stable to reduce forced reflows. Lit invokes the thread ref before the newly rendered inner element is connected, so reading `parentElement` in the callback permanently captured `null`. The virtualizer then had no scroll owner and left appended rows at the same transform.

This change stores the inner thread element and resolves its scroll parent lazily after the render commit, retaining the stable-ref performance improvement while restoring virtual row positioning.

## User Impact

Newly appended Control UI messages now appear below existing transcript rows without requiring a reload.

## Verification

- Regression reproduced on merged `main`: the focused browser test measured a persistent `-184px` row gap.

AI-assisted: yes. The complete branch diff was reviewed with the repo autoreview workflow; all accepted/actionable findings were addressed before landing.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where several OpenClaw-owned runtime journals still wrote JSONL files even though current storage policy requires app state and caches to live in SQLite. Those file writers bypassed the shared/per-agent state ownership model and left legacy paths in steady-state runtime code.

The session/transcript store was deliberately excluded because #98236 owns that SQLite flip.

## Why This Change Was Made

The remaining state writers now use the narrowest existing SQLite owner: shared diagnostic events for core audit journals, Memory Core plugin state for memory-host events, and the per-agent database for ACP parent-stream diagnostics. Legacy persistent audit/event files import only through explicit `openclaw doctor --fix` migrations. Core and plugin doctor imports require exclusive state ownership for their full read/import/archive window, preflight SQLite capacity, verify imported rows, sanitize retired sources, and only then archive them. ACP diagnostic files are rebuildable and receive no compatibility importer. There are no runtime fallback readers or dual writes.

### Audit classification

| Surface | Observed role | Policy classification | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/config/io.audit.ts` (`logs/config-audit.jsonl`) | Core config-write/observe audit writer | Shared state DB, `diagnostic_events` / `config-audit` | Migrated; redacted records; bounded to latest 50,000 rows; legacy import and archive owned by doctor only |
| `src/system-agent/audit.ts` (`audit/system-agent.jsonl`, retired Crestodian path) | Core system-agent mutation audit writer | Shared state DB, `diagnostic_events` / `system-agent-audit` | Migrated; bounded to latest 50,000 rows; legacy import and archive owned by doctor only |
| `src/memory-host-sdk/events.ts` (`memory/.dreams/events.jsonl`) | Memory recall/promotion/dream event state consumed by status, public artifacts, and Memory Wiki | Memory Core plugin KV in shared SQLite | Migrated with atomic cursor + event + retention writes, namespace-global ordering, 8 KiB payload and 10,000-row bounds, and isolated cursor state capped at 1,000 rows; doctor validates the full source, preflights capacity, and defers all import on malformed or unsafe input |
| `memory/events/memory-host-events.jsonl` | Public memory-event artifact consumed by Memory Wiki and bridge clients | Named, derived export artifact; SQLite remains authoritative | Preserved as a real filesystem path for existing consumers; latest 1,000 events, capped at 1 MiB; atomically refreshed only when content changes |
| `src/agents/acp-spawn-parent-stream.ts` (`*.acp-stream.jsonl`) | Child-session ACP parent-stream diagnostic state | Per-agent DB, `acp_parent_stream_events` | Migrated; rows are session-owned and cascade on session deletion; writes batch synchronously, retry with backoff, and cap pending diagnostics; old transient files are not imported |
| `src/infra/session-cost-usage.ts` | Reads legacy/archive transcript JSONL; rollups already use per-agent SQLite | Excluded session/transcript area; no JSONL writer | Left unchanged; #98236 owns session/transcript storage |
| `src/security/fix.ts` | Repairs permissions on excluded transcript artifacts | Excluded session/transcript maintenance; no writer | Left unchanged |
| `src/infra/backup-volatile-filter.ts` and backup creation paths | Backup inputs, filters, and restorable archives | Named backup artifact | Preserved; unimported legacy audit tails are secret-sanitized into the backup, completed blank append pads are omitted, and transient raw checkpoints are removed from the SQLite snapshot |
| `src/agents/cache-trace.ts`, `src/agents/anthropic-payload-log.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.raw-stream.ts`, `src/logging/diagnostic-*`, channel delivery trace | Explicit opt-in traces, raw provider capture, or support bundles | Named diagnostic/log artifacts | Left unchanged |
| CLI runner/Claude session files, transcript/session-manager paths, hooks, compaction checkpoints, session inspection/branching | Provider/external-tool contracts or the excluded session/transcript surface | External tool contract or #98236-owned session artifact | Left unchanged |
| `src/trajectory/{runtime-file,paths,cleanup,types}.ts` | SQLite runtime plus explicit trajectory export/legacy discovery | Named export artifact; no steady-state JSONL app-state writer | Left unchanged |
| `src/infra/{exec-host,exec-approvals}.ts` and node CLI JSONL references | Framed IPC/socket payloads | External wire contract, not file state | Left unchanged |
| `src/plugin-sdk/api-baseline.ts` | Generated SDK inspection output | Generated developer artifact | Left unchanged; tracked checksum regenerated for this SDK surface |
| Schema/help/status/tool-display/workshop references and test-support/harness files from discovery | Format names, readers, fixtures, or temporary external/session scratch | No remaining production file writer | Left unchanged |

The post-change discovery still finds legacy migration constants and legitimate artifact/wire/session references, but no additional non-session OpenClaw-owned runtime JSONL writer.

## User Impact

Operators get one SQLite-backed ownership model for these journals, deterministic cleanup with session deletion, bounded audit retention, and explicit doctor repair for persistent legacy files. Existing backup, support-bundle, provider-log, export, and wire-format artifacts keep their documented behavior.

target.title: fix: Control UI loads unstyled after a gateway update with no way to recover
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Control UI could render as a fully unstyled page (plain links, no layout) after a gateway in-place update, with no recovery offered. The built `index.html` links one hashed entry stylesheet; when a dist swap leaves that URL 404ing while the app JS still boots, none of the existing safety nets fire: `vite:preloadError` only covers dynamic imports, the index.html mount fallback only checks that the app custom element defined, and WKWebView navigation delegates only see top-level document failures.

## Why This Change Was Made

Detection is a CSS sentinel (`:root { --openclaw-css-ok: 1 }` in the entry stylesheet) checked once the document finishes loading, plus a capture-phase stylesheet `error` listener as an early signal. Recovery deliberately reuses the existing stale-chunk machinery — `scheduleStaleChunkReload` already encapsulates the one-auto-reload-per-build-id guard and the gateway HEAD probe — so a transient stale-asset 404 self-heals invisibly. When auto-reload is unavailable (guard consumed or gateway unreachable), an inline-styled banner with a Reload button appears instead of silently staying broken. No gateway, service-worker, or native-app changes.

## User Impact

A Control UI tab or app WebView that would previously stay unstyled until a manual refresh now reloads itself once against the freshly served document; if that cannot help, users get a visible "Styles failed to load" banner with a Reload button.

## Evidence

- Focused tests: `pnpm test ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.test.ts` — 21/21 passed on Blacksmith Testbox (lease `tbx_01kxt0snadnaa9z6k91czxdx07`), including 6 new behavior tests for sentinel detection, banner escalation, capture-phase link errors, single-shot detection, and uninstall.
- Gates: `pnpm check:changed && pnpm build` green on the same Testbox (exit 0). Control UI startup CSS budget unchanged: 1 request, 41.0 KiB gzip (limit 42.0).
- Autoreview (Codex, gpt-5.6-sol): clean, no actionable findings.

target.title: feat(memory-core): skip tool construction for dreaming narrative subagent runs (no-tools mode from #93756 review guidance)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Dreaming narrative subagent runs (light/deep/REM) generate 80–180 words of prose; `NARRATIVE_SYSTEM_PROMPT` explicitly prohibits tool use — yet every run still constructs the full tool/MCP/LSP surface before the model call.

This implements the fix requested by the maintainer review that closed the 60s→120s timeout-bump PRs ([#93756 closing comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/93756#issuecomment-4723436147)): *"an explicit no-tools subagent mode for these narrative-only runs, forwarded into the runner's existing empty-tool fast path."* The issue that tracked it (#92494) was closed without the mode being built; this PR builds it.

`disableTools: true` is threaded from the plugin call site through plugin→gateway→command→embedded-runner, landing in the runner's existing fast path (`resolveEmbeddedAttemptToolConstructionPlan` → `constructTools: false`; MCP/LSP bundle runtimes short-circuit).

## Changes

- **`dreaming-narrative.ts`**: `subagent.run({ …, disableTools: true })` (unconditional — narrative runs never need tools; no config surface, per the `commitments` precedent `{ disableTools: true }` in heartbeat-runner)
- **`SubagentRunParams`** (`plugins/runtime/types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`server-plugins.ts`**: forward flag into `AgentRunRequest`
- **`AgentRunRequest`** (`agent-request-types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`agent-run-execution-phase.ts`**: pass to `AgentCommandIngressOpts`
- **`AgentCommandOpts`** (`command/types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`attempt-execution.ts`**: `disableTools: opts.modelRun === true || opts.disableTools === true`
- **`packages/gateway-protocol/…/agent.ts`**: `disableTools: Type.Optional(Type.Boolean())` in `AgentParamsSchema` (closed object — the field must exist to pass `validateAgentParams` even for internal callers; found via live testing, see Evidence)
- **`agent-request-preflight.ts`**: plugin-only enforcement guard — requests carrying `disableTools` without a server-side `pluginRuntimeOwnerId` get `INVALID_REQUEST` (identical pattern to the existing `cwd` guard directly above it)

**Security:** external callers cannot use the flag — the preflight guard rejects `disableTools` from any request lacking a server-side `pluginRuntimeOwnerId` with `INVALID_REQUEST`, mirroring the existing `cwd` reserved-parameter guard (note: neither guard has direct unit coverage upstream today; happy to add a preflight test harness if wanted).

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (live sandbox — actual Dream Diary path)

Sandboxed gateway built from this branch (merged with upstream/main `b42dc72851`, which includes #110193), mock OpenAI provider logging verbatim request bodies, memory-core dreaming enabled, seeded memory fragments. The **managed dreaming cron fired and `runLightDreaming` dispatched a real narrative subagent run** (session `dreaming-narrative-light-…`, prompt opens "Write a dream diary entry from these memory fragments…"):

- **Narrative request (dreaming path): NO `tools` key, NO `tool_choice`.** Top-level keys `["model","messages","stream","stream_options","max_completion_tokens"]`; total **15,065 bytes**.
- **Control (same gateway session, ordinary heartbeat turn): `tools` array with 25+ schemas, 74,499 bytes** — the flag is surgical; only narrative runs are affected.
- Proof captured on final head `e887c0c6fd`; branch freshly merged against upstream/main `b42dc72851`.

Live testing also surfaced (and this PR now fixes) a validation gap in the original head: `AgentParamsSchema` is a closed object, so the flag was rejected by `validateAgentParams` for **all** callers before any ownership check — the schema addition + preflight guard above are the result. Two sandbox-setup notes for reviewers reproducing: the dreaming config key is `frequency` (not `cron`), and the managed cron registers only when `dreaming.enabled && phases.deep.enabled`.

## Quantified impact (local-model installs)

Measured: tools payload 72,072 chars ≈ **~18K tokens** (chars/4 heuristic). On a measured local reference box (Strix Halo / gfx1151 unified memory, 122B MoE via llama.cpp: prompt prefill ~200 tok/s measured via ~100K-token cold prefill in ~7m49s; generation 15–25 tok/s):

| | tool construction (host) | tool-schema prefill | narrative prefill + generation | total vs 60s wait |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **before** | ~57s cold (measured on ARM, #93756) | ~90s (18K tok ÷ 200 tok/s) | ~25–45s | far past the 60s `NARRATIVE_TIMEOUT_MS` (#101603) |
| **after (this PR)** | skipped | 0 | ~25–45s | near/under the wall |

Three narrative phases per night → several minutes saved per sweep on local installs, and materially less KV/context pressure (#95746). Note the after-column still brushes 60s on modest hardware — this PR **composes with** the configurable timeout in #78440 rather than replacing it. (Estimated figures labeled; tool-surface size varies by install — MCP-heavy setups are worse than 26 tools.)

## Considered alternative: keep tools for prefix-cache sharing

Retaining the tool block so narrative runs share a KV-cache prefix with other run types was considered and rejected: (1) the host-side bundle-tools construction cost is unaffected by any server-side cache; (2) cross-run-type cache hits need byte-identical prefixes, which narrative runs break early anyway (distinct narrative system prompt/bootstrap context); (3) the caching that does occur in practice — the three narrative phases sharing a prefix with each other within a sweep — survives this change with a smaller shared prefix; (4) for per-token cloud providers the unused tool block is strictly wasted spend. No-tools is better for both deployment classes.

### Test plan

- [x] `dreaming-narrative.test.ts`: 30/30 (TDD — red first, then green)
- [x] `server-plugins.test.ts`: 72/72 (includes forward + external-schema-rejection coverage)
- [x] Typecheck (`run-tsgo`) clean; `git diff --check` clean
- [x] Live sandbox: 26 tools / 72,072 chars → no tools / 366 chars
- [x] E2E cron-fired narrative on a live gateway: managed dreaming cron → `runLightDreaming` → real narrative subagent request with no tools (capture above)

Refs: implements #93756 review guidance · context #92494 · composes with #78440 · should relieve #95746

target.title: fix(reef): add timeout and bounded JSON reads to relay transport
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Reef relay transport client (`extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`) calls `fetch` with no timeout. A relay that black-holes the TCP/TLS handshake or stalls before returning headers will hang `ReefInboxConnection.drain()` forever, silently killing the reconnect/backoff loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

This follows the same pattern as recent merged fixes that bound network operations (e.g., #106035, #105885, #102865). The change wraps relay requests in `fetchWithTimeout` (15 s) using the existing injectable `fetcher`, so tests can stub stalled responses. Bounded JSON response reads already landed on `main` via #106456 (16 MiB success / 64 KiB error caps through `readProviderJsonResponse`); this PR adds only the missing request timeout on top of them.

## User Impact

- Prevents silent channel death when the Reef relay becomes unresponsive.
- No behavior change for healthy relays; a stall surfaces as a `TimeoutError` at the 15 s deadline and triggers the existing reconnect path.

## Evidence

- New test covers a stalled relay timing out after 15 s; existing main-side tests cover the bounded JSON reads.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --run` — 10/10 tests passed on the exact head.
- Exact-head controlled-relay proof (real loopback HTTP+WS server, no fetch mocks): healthy pull succeeds; a stalled pre-header request aborts at 15080 ms with `TimeoutError`; a 16 MiB+1 JSON body is rejected with `reef.relay: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes`; after relay 500s the inbox backoff loop recovers, drains the backlog, connects the live socket, and receives the pushed entry. Full transcript in the comments.

target.title: fix(ollama): strip unconsumed response body on non-OK HTTP responses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`checkOllamaCloudAuth`, `pullOllamaModelCore`, and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` in `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` return/throw on non-OK HTTP responses without consuming or cancelling the response body. The `release()` callback from `fetchWithSsrFGuard` also does not cancel the body — it only calls `cleanup()` and `closeDispatcher()`. This leaves undici connections and body streams open, causing resource leaks on every non-OK response.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adds `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => {})` at three call sites before each early return/throw. This releases undici resources immediately rather than relying on GC finalizers or dispatcher teardown. The `.catch(() => {})` is deliberate — a failed cancel must not mask the original error or change the return shape.

## User Impact

Ollama provider instances that encounter non-OK responses (e.g. cloud auth returning 500, model pull failures, model inspection errors) no longer leak body stream resources.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (loopback server)

The proof uses a continuous chunked body stream (interval-based writes every 1ms) to prevent undici from buffering the entire response. Without the fix, the body stream stays open indefinitely while the server keeps writing bytes. With the fix, `body?.cancel()` closes the connection within single-digit milliseconds.

```
$ node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  ok: response body stream is cancelled
  info: bytes_written_before_cancel=2048 elapsed_ms=239
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 4 passed, 0 failed
```

### Mutation check

Revert the 3 `response.body?.cancel()` lines → body is NOT cancelled:

```
$ git stash && node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  FAIL: response body stream is cancelled
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 3 passed, 1 failed
```

Restore fix → 4/4 passed.

### Vitest

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  38 passed (38)
```

### Format check

```
$ oxfmt --check extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.
```

### Not tested

- Live Ollama cloud auth API roundtrip with real credentials
- `pullOllamaModelCore` and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` paths (internal functions; same body-cancel pattern applied)
- `release()` integration with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` dispatcher lifecycle

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Some deployments serve a Claude/MiniMax model through a proxy that intermittently degrades a native `tool_use` block into plain text. In that degraded case the tool call arrives as the namespaced/bare XML attribute dialect — `<invoke name="tool"><parameter name="x">v</parameter></invoke>`, optionally wrapped in `<function_calls>...</function_calls>` and optionally prefixed with `antml:` or `mm:`.

On current `main` two gaps remained:

1. The visible-text sanitizer recognized the `antml:` prefix but not the `mm:` prefix, so a degraded `mm:invoke` block leaked verbatim into the user-visible reply.
2. The persist-path stripper (`packages/tool-call-repair` `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) did not recognize the attribute-dialect invoke at all, so an unfenced standalone degraded invoke block was written into the durable `done.message` instead of being scrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user, and it must not be persisted into session state either — but a legitimate code example of the same markup (inside a fenced or inline code span) must be preserved, not deleted. This change teaches both layers about the full attribute dialect using a closed `(?:antml:|mm:)?` namespace allow-list, so arbitrary `ns:` tokens in prose are never matched.

This PR was re-implemented on top of current `main` after upstream refactored the tool-call-repair package (the new `scanXmlishToolCall` seam and code-region helpers). The change is scoped to the net delta that still reproduces on `main`:

- **Visible text** (`assistant-visible-text.ts`): mirror the existing `antml:` handling for the `mm:` namespace in the tag-name scan, quick-check, and payload-start patterns. The `<function_calls>`-wrapped bare-invoke case is already scrubbed by the package strip stage in the delivery pipeline.
- **Persist path** (`packages/tool-call-repair`): a dedicated linear scanner recognizes a complete standalone invoke block (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `<function_calls>` wrapper, self-closing, and zero-parameter forms). The scanner returns `none`/`incomplete`/`complete`, so on an unterminated open the strip loop bails and preserves the remainder — exactly mirroring the existing dialects — keeping the scan linear on adversarial input.
- **Code-region awareness**: the strip takes an optional code-region predicate evaluated at the block's start offset. Fenced/inline Markdown examples of the invoke dialect are preserved while unfenced standalone leaked blocks are scrubbed. Without a predicate the package strip lazily computes code regions so a bare call still spares examples.
- **Plugin SDK contract preserved**: the exported `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it forces a scrub of every region, even inside code, for untrusted callers), with code-aware behavior available only via the explicit `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` opt-in.
- **Layering**: `findCodeRegions`/`isInsideCode`/`CodeRegion` were moved into `normalization-core` (the package's only dependency) so `tool-call-repair` can share one implementation without importing app source; `src/shared/text/code-regions.ts` re-exports them so existing callers are unaffected.

Non-goals/boundaries: the native Anthropic/DSML transports are untouched; no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced; the equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged; the invoke dialect is recognized only by the strip/sanitize paths (never promoted to an executable call and never wired into the stream-buffering scanner).

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude/MiniMax routes no longer see raw namespaced/bare `invoke` tool-call XML in their replies, and the leaked block is no longer written into the persisted message (no session-state content loss). Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped. A resolved-review audit also removed an O(n²) worst case on the persist strip path, so adversarial degraded text cannot cause pathological CPU use.

## Evidence

Focused regression tests were added at the layers that own the contract:
- `packages/tool-call-repair/src/payload.test.ts`: invoke-dialect variants (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `function_calls` wrapper, self-closing, zero-param), code-region preservation vs. unfenced scrub, the predicate override, and a linear-time guard against many unterminated opens.
- `src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts`: the `preserveCodeRegions` opt-in and strict default.
- `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`: the `mm:invoke`/`mm:parameter` visible-text case (parallel to the existing `antml:` case), alongside existing standalone-vs-inline `function_calls` delivery-path coverage.

Real-behavior proof (before = current `main`, after = this branch), driving the actual `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` and `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` on the leak shapes:

```
=== BEFORE (main) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it.\n<mm:invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<mm:parameter name=\"city\">Paris</mm:parameter>\n</mm:invoke>"
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done.\n<function_calls>\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>\n</function_calls>"
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (preserved)

=== AFTER (this branch) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it."
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done."
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (still preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (still preserved)
```

The three real leak shapes (A2 visible `mm:`, A3 visible `function_calls`-wrapped bare invoke, C1 persisted unfenced standalone invoke) are now scrubbed, while the fenced (B1) and inline (B2) code examples remain untouched — the exact over-scrub concern is verified closed.

O(n²) audit fix: a resolved-review pass measured the persist strip degrading quadratically on adversarial input with many unterminated invoke opens (720 KB ≈ 977 ms, scaling to seconds for a few MB). Making the scanner bail on `incomplete` (mirroring the existing unterminated-candidate bail) brought the same 720 KB input to ≈ 0.8 ms and restored linear scaling; a regression test locks this.

Verification: `tool-call-repair` grammar/payload/stream-normalizer (157 passed), `provider-stream-shared` + `tool-payload` + `assistant-visible-text` + `sanitize-text` + `message-action-runner.send-validation` + `embedded-agent-utils` (all green), `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` exit 0, `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` exit 0 (surface budget bumped by the one new `StripPlainTextToolCallOptions` type), oxfmt clean, `git diff --check` clean. Rebased onto current `main` (`9b823c61`).

target.title: fix(memory): reject malformed embedding batch JSONL bytes
target.body:
﻿<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

AI-assisted: yes. This PR was prepared with Codex assistance.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running memory embedding batch workflows could have malformed provider JSONL output accepted after invalid UTF-8 bytes were rewritten as replacement characters.

The affected path is the shared embedding batch output reader used by the OpenAI, Gemini, and Voyage batch readers. When a provider output line was otherwise valid JSON, a bad byte inside a string could become a `U+FFFD` replacement character before `JSON.parse`, which could corrupt fields such as `custom_id` or provider error text instead of reporting a malformed batch record.

## Why This Change Was Made

The batch output reader now decodes each JSONL record with fatal UTF-8 handling and maps decode failures to the existing malformed-record error shape. This keeps the fix at the shared JSONL boundary and leaves the existing record byte cap, physical-record counting, stream cancellation, and provider-specific output-line handling unchanged.

This is not a vector/embedding metadata schema change and does not alter persisted embedding rows, metadata shape, or migration behavior. It only rejects malformed provider output bytes before those bytes can become parsed JSON records.

## User Impact

Malformed embedding batch output now fails clearly as a malformed JSONL record instead of silently carrying corrupted replacement characters into memory embedding result processing. Valid UTF-8 JSONL output continues to parse as before across OpenAI, Gemini, and Voyage batch readers.

## Evidence

Runtime proof from the embedding-batch provider path:

```text
Command:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-provider-openai.config.ts extensions/openai/pr110502-real-proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose

Setup:
Temporary, uncommitted proof test on PR head ec24fc526094.
A local OpenAI-compatible loopback HTTP server handled the same batch flow used by runOpenAiEmbeddingBatches(...): upload file, create completed batch, then download /files/{output_file_id}/content. No live OpenAI API key or production credential was used.

Valid provider output:
[runtime proof] valid server=http://127.0.0.1:62448/v1
[runtime proof] valid path: POST /v1/files -> POST /v1/batches -> GET /v1/files/output-1/content
[runtime proof] valid result: [["req-1",[0.1,0.2]]]

Malformed provider output:
[runtime proof] malformed server=http://127.0.0.1:62452/v1
[runtime proof] malformed path: POST /v1/files -> POST /v1/batches -> GET /v1/files/output-1/content
[runtime proof] malformed bytes: 0xc3 0x28 inside provider JSONL string
[runtime proof] malformed result: openai.batch-file-content: malformed JSONL record

Result:
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       2 passed (2)
```

This proof exercises `runOpenAiEmbeddingBatches(...)` and the provider batch-output download path rather than calling `readEmbeddingBatchJsonl(...)` directly. The OpenAI-compatible batch flow matches the output-file shape used by provider batch APIs: completed batch metadata points to an output file, and the reader downloads `/files/{output_file_id}/content` before parsing JSONL records.

Focused validation:

```text
pnpm test packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts extensions/openai/embedding-batch.test.ts extensions/google/embedding-batch.test.ts extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.test.ts
```

Passed: 4 focused Vitest test files/suites covering the shared JSONL reader plus OpenAI, Google/Gemini, and Voyage embedding batch callers.

Additional checks:

```text
pnpm exec oxfmt --check packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.ts packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts
git diff --check
```

Both passed. Full local `pnpm build && pnpm check && pnpm test` was not run; the focused validation above covers the touched reader and its provider callers, and GitHub CI is running the broader lanes.

The new regression test in `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts` feeds invalid UTF-8 bytes (`0xc3, 0x28`) inside a JSONL string and verifies the reader rejects it as `test.batch-output: malformed JSONL record`. It covers both newline-terminated records and an unterminated final record.

User-realistic proof / call chain:

```text
User runs a memory embedding batch workflow
-> provider batch output is downloaded by the OpenAI, Google/Gemini, or Voyage embedding batch reader
-> extensions/openai/embedding-batch.ts, extensions/google/embedding-batch.ts, or extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.ts calls readEmbeddingBatchJsonl(...)
-> packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.ts decodes each provider JSONL record
-> invalid UTF-8 now throws before JSON.parse(...)
-> provider-specific embedding result handling only receives valid decoded JSON objects
```

The focused test covers the shared reader where provider JSONL bytes first become text, and the provider embedding batch test files were rerun to check the sibling OpenAI, Google/Gemini, and Voyage callers still accept valid JSONL output.

Dependency contract checked: `TextDecoder(utf-8, { fatal: true })` throws on malformed data instead of replacing bad bytes with `U+FFFD`; the PR relies on that built-in decoder behavior to fail closed before `JSON.parse`.

target.title: fix(ios): prevent black edge bands in chat
target.body:
Closes #110503

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where iOS users in dark appearance saw message content meet opaque black bands at the top navigation bar and bottom composer after the native navigation redesign.

## Why This Change Was Made

The iOS host now lets the shared layered chat canvas extend behind its chrome instead of covering it with `systemBackground`. On iOS 26, descendant vertical scroll views use the native soft edge effect; earlier iOS versions retain their existing edge behavior.

## User Impact

Chat once again reads as one continuous translucent surface. Messages transition softly beneath the navigation and composer chrome without changing composer behavior, routing, or conversation state.

## Evidence

- Before: the dark fixture's empty canvas measured `0.0` layered pixels and rendered as a solid-black surface.
- After: the same fixture passes a pixel-level layered-canvas assertion, sends a message, receives the fixture response, and captures the bottom-edge state.
- `OpenClawSnapshotUITests.testChatKeepsLayeredCanvasInDarkAppearance` passes on iPhone 17 Pro / iOS 26.5.
- `OpenClawSnapshotUITests.testChatComposerStartsCompactAndGrowsWithDraft` and `testChatPresentationInLightAppearance` pass on the same simulator.
- The new `RootTabsSourceGuardTests` edge-treatment guard passed; the full source-guard run on the earlier base exposed three unrelated stale expectations.
- Changed-gate proof passed on Blacksmith Testbox: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29634870411
- Source-blind behavior contract passed for dark canvas continuity, message send/reply, and light-appearance preservation.

AI-assisted with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and ran the repository autoreview gate; no actionable findings remained.
