target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

## What Problem This Solves

Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading, caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, block the loop for 14-22 seconds and drop messages (issue #87509 reports 14-22s bootstrap-context stalls that block channel I/O, WebSocket keepalive, and timers).

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

## Why This Change Was Made

Bootstrap extra-file loading runs during embedded-run bootstrap-context, on the hot path that prepares every agent turn. On `main` the exported loader reaches Node `fs.glob` and synchronous fd reads, which monopolize the event loop over a large workspace; this change routes the same exported loader through an async yielding walker and async fd reads, and yields between bootstrap hook handlers, so channel I/O stays responsive during bootstrap. The public plugin SDK surface is deliberately unchanged.

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Preserve `fs.glob` explicit directory-symlink parity: descend a symlink only when its aligned pattern segment is literal (non-wildcard) and `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace root, so an explicit configured pattern like `linked/**/AGENTS.md` still reaches descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink. Symlinks reached through a wildcard segment stay terminal (matching `fs.glob`), workspace containment rejects symlink targets that escape the root, and a `realpath` ancestor-chain guard refuses re-entry into a directory already on the descent path so an ancestor-pointing symlink (`a/loop -> a`) cannot loop.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — explicit directory-symlink glob parity across three states (real `fs.symlink`): a literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

## User Impact

Agents whose workspaces contain large trees or broad `bootstrap-extra-files` globs no longer stall the event loop for seconds during bootstrap-context, so WebSocket keepalives, typing indicators, HTTP requests, and timers keep firing while an agent turn is being prepared — messages are no longer dropped. The set of bootstrap files loaded is unchanged (identical glob match set), so no agent sees different context. Root bootstrap file loading goes serial-sync → parallel-async, glob walks go blocking → yielding, and hook chains go uninterrupted → yielded.

## Evidence

This is a **current-`main` vs current-PR-head** real-behavior benchmark against the real exported loader, covering elapsed time, event-loop responsiveness, glob-match parity, and RSS.

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces (issue #87509). This change replaces the native `fs.glob` walk with an async walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries so the event loop stays responsive, while returning the identical configured `bootstrap-extra-files` match set.
- **Real environment tested**: OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. `main` = `9b823c610816` (native `fs.glob`, synchronous fd reads); head = `3dfd7f1d4952` (async yielding walker, async fd reads). The identical benchmark script runs inside each checkout (relative import binds to that checkout's implementation); both consume the same pre-built read-only workspace.
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of **395,807 filesystem entries** (391,124 files, 4,683 dirs — wide flat dirs + a deep 40-level tree + `node_modules` + `.git` + `.hidden` noise), with `AGENTS.md` planted at several depths (root, deep-past-old-cutoff, `.hidden/`, `node_modules/`). Configured pattern `**/AGENTS.md`. During the load a 5ms repeating timer counts liveness ticks, `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay({resolution:5})` records event-loop delay, and `process.memoryUsage().rss` is captured before/after with `global.gc()`. 3 fresh processes per side after a discarded warmup; values below are medians.
- **Failing proof before fix** (current `main` `9b823c610816`, native `fs.glob`):
  ```
  elapsed: 834.5ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 55.5ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 8.50ms   p99: 54.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 95 / 166 expected (57.2% kept)
  rssDelta: 358.3 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: fs.glob finishes the walk fast but monopolizes the loop —
          multi-tens-of-ms stalls, ~43% of 5ms liveness ticks dropped, 358 MB RSS spike
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch** (identical script both sides; full reproduce recipe below):
  ```
  # build the shared 395,807-entry workspace once, then run each side from its own checkout
  node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws"
  ```
- **Evidence after fix** (current PR head `3dfd7f1d4952`, async yielding walker):
  ```
  elapsed: 1244.8ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 10.7ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 5.09ms   p99: 6.6ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 245 / 248 expected (98.8% kept)
  rssDelta: 57.0 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: yielding walker keeps the loop responsive — max delay near the 5ms floor,
          98.8% of liveness ticks fired, RSS footprint ~6x smaller
  ```
- **Glob result parity (main vs head)**: sha256 of the sorted relative match set is **identical** on both sides — `b90d55afa71f2aa871ea40de7d91715377c93b76d26e7f43d817019b6b72a97e`. Matched set both sides: `AGENTS.md`, the deep 40-level `deep/.../AGENTS.md`, and `node_modules/pkg000/AGENTS.md`; `.git` and `.hidden/AGENTS.md` correctly excluded by both. The custom walker changes event-loop behavior and memory, not the returned file set.

  | metric (median of 3, 395,807 entries, Node v24.10.0) | main `9b823c610816` | head `3dfd7f1d4952` |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | elapsed (ms) | 834.5 | 1244.8 |
  | max event-loop delay (ms) | 55.5 | 10.7 |
  | mean event-loop delay (ms) | 8.50 | 5.09 |
  | liveness ticks kept | 57.2% | 98.8% |
  | RSS delta (MB) | 358.3 | 57.0 |
  | `**/AGENTS.md` matches returned | 3 | 3 (identical set) |

- **Observed result after fix**: the fix trades a modest wall-clock increase (834ms → 1245ms) for the property the issue actually needs — the event loop stops stalling. Max event-loop delay drops from 55.5ms to 10.7ms (near the 5ms probe floor), liveness-tick retention rises from 57.2% to 98.8%, and peak RSS is ~6x smaller (358MB → 57MB) because the walker no longer buffers the whole `fs.glob` result eagerly. The returned match set is byte-identical (same sha256), so existing `bootstrap-extra-files` configs load the same files. At the field-report scale (much larger real workspaces), `main`'s blocking walk is what produces the 14-22s embedded_run stalls; this benchmark demonstrates the direction and mechanism (blocking `fs.glob` vs cooperative yielding) at 395,807 entries on a single dev box.
- **Reproduce**:
  ```bash
  BENCH=/tmp/bench-89040
  PR=<pr-head-checkout>
  git -C "$PR" worktree add --detach "$BENCH/main-wt" 9b823c610816   # current upstream/main
  ln -s "$PR/node_modules" "$BENCH/main-wt/node_modules"             # read-only bench, first-party deps
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$PR/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$BENCH/main-wt/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  # build the shared workspace once (reused by both sides, walk mutates nothing)
  (cd "$PR" && node --import tsx/esm "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" build "$BENCH/ws" 400000)
  # 3 fresh processes per side, run from inside each checkout so the relative import binds
  (cd "$PR"            && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  (cd "$BENCH/main-wt" && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  ```
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real exported glob-resolution path (`loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics`) and event-loop instrumentation directly rather than through a connected channel. The main-side `node_modules` is symlinked from the head checkout, which is valid because `workspace.ts`'s transitive imports are first-party and the run is read-only. Focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

### Directory-symlink glob parity proof

- **Behavior addressed**: The cooperative walker only descended `Dirent.isDirectory()` entries and emitted symlinks as leaf candidates, so an explicit configured pattern such as `linked/**/AGENTS.md` no longer reached descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink — Node's `fs.glob` resolves that case, so the walker silently dropped configured bootstrap context. The walker now descends a literal-named path-segment symlink when `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace, keeps wildcard-reached symlinks terminal, and guards against ancestor cycles.
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`. Three regression tests build real temp directories with real `fs.symlink` links and drive the real exported extra-bootstrap glob resolver.
- **Steps run**: `npx vitest run src/agents/workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts src/agents/workspace.test.ts`
- **Observed result**: `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 156 passed (156)`. The three symlink states are covered: (a) literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; (b) a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; (c) an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping (guarded by a 15s timeout). A TDD red check confirmed test (a) fails on the pre-fix walker (missing the `linked/` descendants) and passes after the fix; `tsgo:core` exits 0 and `oxfmt --check` reports both files formatted.
- **What was not tested**: Behavior on Windows/`EPERM`/`ENOSYS` filesystems where symlink creation is unavailable — those cases skip cleanly rather than assert.

Closes #87509

target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate — producing **invalid Unicode in the outbound API request**.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. The fix switches to `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, an existing repo helper.

## Outbound payload proof (real behavior)

Input: 41-code-unit tool call ID with 🐱 surrogate pair at positions 39-40.

### BEFORE fix (`id.slice(0, 40)`) — BROKEN

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\ud83d"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 40 code units, trailing **unpaired high surrogate** `\uD83D`
- Invalid Unicode sent to OpenAI API — downstream rejection risk

```
Output: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa�" (40 units)
Unpaired surrogate at tail: FAIL
```

### AFTER fix (`truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)`) — SAFE

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 39 code units, clean ASCII
- Valid Unicode sent to OpenAI API

```
Output: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" (39 units)
Unpaired surrogate at tail: none (PASS)
Length ≤ 40: PASS
```

**Evidence**: The `onPayload` hook intercepts the exact outbound JSON before `fetch` — the same bytes the OpenAI API receives. The captured payload above is the real API request content.

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` — `slice(0,40)` → `truncateUtf16Safe` |
| **Sibling UTF-16 PRs** | #104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839 — same helper |
| **Callers** | `convertMessages` → `streamOpenAICompletions` — cross-model tool-call path |
| **Test** | 47/47 pass; surrogate-pair boundary test with 41-unit 🐱 input |
| **Mutation proof** | Reverting to `slice` makes test FAIL: `trailing high surrogate: true` |
| **Payload proof** | Captured outbound JSON shows valid `tool_call_id` — no unpaired surrogate |
| **CI** | Rebased onto current `main` |

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider tool-call conversations produce valid Unicode in all IDs
- No change for IDs without surrogate pairs at the 40-unit boundary
- Non-OpenAI provider paths unchanged

target.title: feat(system-agent): auto-hatch into the agent after fresh setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Phase 5 PR2 of the custodian onboarding redesign (plan: `docs/start/onboarding-redesign.md`). After a fresh-install setup applies in the custodian conversation, users were parked in the custodian with a "talk to agent" hint instead of the decided hatch ceremony — the moment the plan calls the identity beat of onboarding.

## Why This Change Was Made

The plan's decided principles: "the hatch is a ceremony" and "zero agents on first run auto-hatches with an announcement". The pieces already shipped — `create-agent`/setup operations, the seeded `BOOTSTRAP.md` birth sequence (phase 5 PR1), the web custodian surface (phase 4) — this PR connects them.

## User Impact

- A fresh-install `setup` apply in the OpenClaw conversation now announces the hatch ("Your agent is hatching — handing you over now. You can always find me in Settings → Ask OpenClaw.") and hands straight off: `open-tui` in the terminal (the TUI backend's existing handoff opens the agent), mapped to `open-agent` for gateway clients.
- The web custodian page turns `open-agent` into a navigation to agent chat with the birth-sequence opener ("Wake up, my friend!" — the same seed the CLI hatch uses) prefilled as a composer draft, so one Send wakes the seeded `BOOTSTRAP` and the agent names itself.
- The hatch fires only on clean post-write verification: if the written config is flagged, the user stays in setup with the warning instead of being dropped into an agent that cannot answer.
- Non-setup persistent operations keep their in-place replies; nothing changes for configured installs (setup does not re-apply there).
- Avatar/image-gen ladder remains a follow-up per the plan.

## Evidence

- Engine suite: 59 tests green, including "hatches into the agent after a fresh setup applies" (announcement + `open-tui` + workspace handoff), "stays in setup when post-write verification flags the config", and "does not hand off when a non-setup persistent operation applies".
- Custodian page: 18 tests green including "hands off to agent chat with the hatch draft on open-agent" (draft URL-encoded); full `ui/src` shard 4393 tests green post-rebase over #110269; `pnpm ui:i18n:baseline`/`verify` green (new key `custodian.hatchDraft`).
- Autoreview (Codex, branch mode, xhigh): clean post-rebase ("patch is correct", 0.87); the one finding during development (unconditional handoff despite failed verification) was fixed with the regression test above.
- Live context: the custodian surfaces around this handoff were live-verified this session (typed welcome cards, caretaker vs onboarding greeting, Exit setup gating). Known gap, stated honestly: the full fresh-install *web* hatch (setup apply → open-agent → draft) was not run live end-to-end — the equivalent CLI hatch path (seeded TUI handoff) was live-tested when phases 2-3 landed, and the web-specific delta is covered by the unit tests above.

target.title: test(agents): add native loopback regression for outer-abort SSE cancellation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Adds native loopback regression coverage proving that the existing outer `AbortSignal` cancels a keepalive-style dripping proxy SSE body in `streamProxy` (`/api/stream`). Without this coverage, a future change to the abort handler or reader cleanup path could silently break total-stream-lifetime ownership without any test catching it.

## Why This Change Was Made

`streamProxy` bounds pre-header waits and per-chunk SSE idle, but the total stream lifetime after headers is owned by the caller's `signal` / outer agent-provider abort budget. A dripping keepalive SSE body (chunks every 20ms) resets per-chunk idle forever, so only the outer abort can terminate it. This PR adds a native loopback regression proving that path works end-to-end with real Node `http` + `fetch` + `ReadableStream`.

An earlier revision proposed an opt-in `streamDeadlineMs` proxy-local wall-clock. ClawSweeper review ([P1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109185#issuecomment-4995322509)) identified that no production caller needed it and the outer `signal` already owns total stream lifetime, so a second deadline source would create a competing timeout contract. This revision removes `streamDeadlineMs` entirely and narrows to the regression proof only (Maintainer option 1, recommended).

Non-goals: adding a proxy-local total-stream deadline; changing the existing outer-abort contract; live proxy provider auth.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `proxy SSE abort`, `streamDeadlineMs`, `proxy stream lifetime`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. This is a test-only PR that protects the existing outer-abort SSE cancellation contract against regressions.

## Verification

- Exact head: `ece303619a791e886a15d94b9723c5a206f5624b`
- `oxfmt --check src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts` - passed; exit 0.
- `oxlint src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts` - passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` - passed; exit 0.

Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.9 /tmp/openclaw-109185

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > reconstructs a text signature from text_start before streamed deltas 366ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > flushes a final SSE frame without a trailing newline 6ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > forwards prompt cache affinity separately from session identity 3ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > applies timeoutMs before proxy response headers arrive 8ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > bounds non-2xx proxy JSON error reads 97ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > caps unterminated pending SSE bytes before a frame delimiter arrives 57ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > caps delimiter-terminated SSE success body bytes 46ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > re-arms the SSE idle timeout after each received chunk 4ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > does not apply the pre-header timeout as an absolute stream deadline 3ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > returns an error result when the SSE read idles 4ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > honors a longer configured SSE read idle timeout 2ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > releases the proxy response reader after a terminal stream 1ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > returns an error result when EOF arrives without a terminal event 1ms
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > cancels a dripping native SSE body when the outer abort signal fires 147ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
   Start at  09:20:33
   Duration  3.38s

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 10.64s
```

Mutation check: temporarily commented out `reader.cancel()` in the `abortHandler` (`src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:287`) -> loopback test fails (1 failed | 13 passed) -> restored -> 14 passed. Proves the regression test catches abort-handler breakage.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: a dripping keepalive SSE body (20ms cadence) that resets per-chunk idle is canceled by the outer `AbortSignal` within 1.5s, not by per-chunk idle (which never fires because drip resets it).

Real environment tested: Linux, Node 22, real `http.createServer` loopback on `127.0.0.1`, real `fetch` / `ReadableStream` (no mocked reader or fetch).

Exact commands run:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

Observed output:

```text
✓ |agents| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > cancels a dripping native SSE body when the outer abort signal fires 147ms

Tests  14 passed (14)
```

Evidence:
- Drip cadence: 20ms (resets per-chunk idle every 20ms; idle timeout 10s never fires)
- Outer abort latency: < 1,500ms (asserted; observed 147ms)
- Cancellation result: `stopReason: "aborted"`, `errorMessage: "Request aborted by user"`
- All 14 tests pass including 13 existing proxy tests (no regression)
- Mutation check: removing `reader.cancel()` from abort handler -> test fails -> restored -> passes

What was not tested: live remote proxy provider outage with provider credentials; non-HTTP/1.1 transports; proxy auth flows.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. Test-only change; no production code modified. No new API surface, config, or behavior contract. The regression test uses native Node `http` + `fetch` on loopback, matching the production `streamProxy` code path.

target.title: fix(models): clear stale auth cooldowns after early limit resets
target.body:
Related: #70903

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who resolve a provider usage or billing condition before its recorded reset time can remain stuck on fallback because the saved auth profile is still locally blocked.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a profile-scoped `openclaw models auth clear-cooldown <profile-id>` command that reuses the existing locked reset operation, targets the persisted owner of inherited profiles, verifies the authoritative stored result, and prints the safe-restart step needed to discard live Gateway bookkeeping. It deliberately does not add polling, shorten provider backoffs, change fallback policy, restart services implicitly, or remove credentials.

## User Impact

Operators can safely re-evaluate a recovered provider without editing SQLite or repeating OAuth. If the underlying failure still applies, the next request can restore the cooldown normally.

## Evidence

target.title: fix: prevent repeated tool-call IDs from poisoning sessions
target.body:
Closes #109443

Related prior candidate: #109447

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where sessions using providers that reuse tool-call IDs across assistant turns could lose legitimate tool results during replay. The resulting malformed payload caused strict providers such as Kimi to reject every later model call until the session was reset.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared transcript repair now pairs calls and results by occurrence within assistant-turn frames instead of treating raw provider IDs as transcript-global identities. Local results stay with their frame, same-turn repeated IDs use FIFO occurrence pairing, failed frames retain ownership of their results, and displaced results move only when exactly one unresolved occurrence can own them.

Pairing also runs before provider-specific ID rewriting, so rewritten call and result IDs remain aligned. Ambiguous displaced output is deliberately dropped and replaced with a synthetic result rather than attributed to the wrong call.

This is an independently validated alternative to #109447 with conservative ambiguity handling and explicit same-turn duplicate coverage.

## User Impact

Sessions can continue normally when providers restart tool-call numbering on later turns. Valid histories no longer become permanently poisoned by replay repair, and missing-result recovery remains deterministic without guessing between ambiguous repeated IDs.

No configuration, schema, migration, or operator action is required.

## Evidence

- Final focused validation on rebased HEAD: 238 tests passed across transcript repair, transport replay, ID sanitization, attempt normalization, and session-history integration.
- Full exact-diff changed gate passed: production/test typechecks, formatting, plugin boundaries, full core/UI/package/scripts lint, import-cycle checks, and storage/security guards.
- Fresh pre-commit autoreview: clean, with no accepted/actionable findings. Its initial same-turn duplicate-ID finding was fixed and re-reviewed.
- Live committed-fix proof on Kimi `k3`: five repeated calls retained five results; provider returned HTTP 200 and completed normally. https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_063dc8c4f315
- Frozen-main negative control: the same repair pipeline reduced five results to one, and Kimi returned HTTP 400 for the corresponding missing-result contract. https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_d8e186434006
- Rebased from `3d1b77103511` to current `origin/main` with an unchanged stable patch ID, then reran focused validation.

AI-assisted by Codex. I reviewed the implementation, invariants, tests, upstream Codex normalization behavior, and live provider evidence.

target.title: fix(openai): bound blob websocket message reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Codex WebSocket streaming accepts message payloads from browser/runtime WebSocket implementations. String and typed-array messages already arrive as bounded in-memory frames, but Blob-like messages were decoded by calling `arrayBuffer()` directly. When the Blob-like object exposes a `size`, an oversized message could still force a whole-body read before the provider surfaced a protocol error.

## Why This Change Was Made

`decodeWebSocketData()` now checks Blob-like `size` before reading and rechecks the decoded `ArrayBuffer.byteLength` afterward. Both checks use the existing ChatGPT Responses success-body cap, keeping the normal string and typed-array paths unchanged while bounding the non-string Blob-like fallback.

## User Impact

Oversized Blob-like Codex WebSocket messages now fail fast with `Codex WebSocket message exceeded size limit` instead of being fully buffered first. Valid WebSocket response messages continue to decode normally.

## Evidence

Branch: `codex/audit-websocket-blob-cap-v2` | Base: `origin/main`

### Regression Test

Added `rejects oversized blob-like websocket messages before reading them` in `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts`. The test injects a WebSocket message whose `data` is a Blob-like object with an oversized `size`, then verifies the stream fails through the size-limit error without calling `arrayBuffer()`.

### Runtime Evidence (Direct Function Test)

Added `blob-websocket-direct-proof.test.ts` which imports and tests the **actual** `decodeWebSocketData` function with real Node.js `Blob` objects:

```
✓ rejects oversized Blob-like object BEFORE arrayBuffer() call
✓ decodes valid Blob-like object successfully
✓ second check catches fake size that passes first check
✓ handles boundary case at exact limit
```

**Test output:**
```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  4 passed (4)
```

**What this proves:**
- **Oversized Blob-like objects** (16MB + 1) are rejected **before** `arrayBuffer()` is called
- **Valid Blob-like objects** (small SSE messages) decode successfully through the actual code path
- **Second byteLength check** catches cases where `size` is faked but actual data is oversized
- **Boundary case** at exactly 16MB passes both checks

### Local checks


target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` in `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` to prevent prototype pollution when config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` function in `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75` iterates over source config entries and checks whether each key is absent from the runtime config. The check uses the `in` operator, which traverses the prototype chain. If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property name (e.g. `"toString"`, `"constructor"`), `!(key in runtime)` incorrectly returns `false`, causing the code to enter the recursive `else` branch and call `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(sourceValue, runtime[key])` where `runtime[key]` resolves to a prototype function.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75`, `!(key in runtime)` uses the `in` operator on a plain config object where `key` comes from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data.

## Root Cause
- The `in` operator traverses the prototype chain; `Object.hasOwn` checks only own properties
- Config keys come from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data
- The same function uses `Object.keys()` (own properties only) for iterating, creating an inconsistency
- The same file already has `Object.hasOwn(value, "$include")` at line 85 — this site was missed (path drift)

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Consistent**: The same file uses `Object.hasOwn` at line 85 for `"$include"` and at lines 41-42 in `createMergePatch`
- **Zero overhead**: Identical performance characteristics
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503

## User Impact
- **Before**: A config key named `toString` or `constructor` would bypass the "new key" check and enter recursive projection with a prototype function
- **After**: Prototype-named keys are correctly treated as absent from runtime and kept as-is

## Evidence
- **Before**: `!("toString" in {})` returns `false` (prototype pollution causes wrong branch)
- **After**: `!Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` returns `true` (correct — treated as new key)
- Regression test added: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
// With '!(key in runtime)': 'toString' in {} → true (prototype)
// Goes to else branch with runtime['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString
console.log('FAIL: typeof result.toString:', typeof result.toString);
"
# typeof result.toString: function (should be string)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
console.log('PASS: result.toString:', result.toString);
"
# result.toString: my-value
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/io.write-prepare.test.ts` — 54 tests passed (53 existing + 1 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression test: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

target.title: fix(tts): defer text settlement for final-mode TTS to eliminate churn (#83511)
target.body:
## Summary

When `messages.tts.mode = "final"`, the Telegram bot exhibited text "churn" — users would briefly see a text message appear, then it would be deleted and replaced by a voice note with the same text as caption. This happened on **both** the ACP dispatch path and the non-ACP dispatch path (`dispatch-from-config.ts`).

This PR eliminates the churn on **both paths** by introducing a `captionedFinalText` channel capability, suppressing live block delivery and partial streaming when captioned final TTS will be used, and correctly handling tagged auto-TTS mode with a split eligibility boolean.

## Root cause

```
Before (main):
  1. Block text / partial streaming delivers text to user immediately
  2. TTS synthesis runs (2-5 seconds)
  3. Voice note + caption delivered as separate message
  Result: user sees text first, then voice note = churn (#83511)

After (this PR):
  1. willUseCaptionedFinalTts = true (channel supports captioned voice + final TTS mode)
  2. Partial streaming suppressed, block text delivery suppressed
  3. TTS synthesis runs, text accumulated silently
  4. Voice note + caption delivered as single message (or text fallback if TTS fails)
  Result: user sees only the voice note with caption = no churn
```

### Tagged auto-TTS mode

When `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"`, TTS only fires for replies containing `[[tts:...]]` directives. Three additional issues were discovered and fixed:

1. **Split boolean**: `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` was doing two jobs — gating live text suppression AND caption eligibility. Split into `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` (live text suppression, excludes tagged) and `canCaptionFinalTts` (caption eligibility, includes tagged).

2. **Block TTS gate**: The accumulated block TTS fallback was gated on `replies.length === 0`, but Anthropic streaming returns both block callbacks and a final reply payload. Changed to gate on `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` and `queuedFinal` instead.

3. **Partial streaming leak**: `onPartialReply` was active for tagged mode, sending raw `[[tts:text]]...[[/tts:text]]` directive text to Telegram during streaming, creating a duplicate text message before the voice+caption arrived. Fixed by gating `onPartialReply` with `canCaptionFinalTts` (covers both always and tagged modes) instead of `willUseCaptionedFinalTts`.

### Media block preservation

When captioned final TTS is active, block suppression is narrowed to **text-only** payloads. Blocks containing media (`mediaUrl`, `mediaUrls`), `presentation`, `interactive`, or `channelData` are delivered immediately with their text stripped (to avoid duplicating the caption). This applies to both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` + `canCaptionFinalTts`: suppress partial streaming and block text for both always and tagged modes; narrow block suppression to text-only payloads (media blocks delivered with text stripped); `sendFinalPayload` returns `deliveredMedia`; block TTS gate changed from `replies.length === 0` to `!deliveredFinalTtsMedia && !queuedFinal` |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts` | Regression tests: tagged directive-only voice+caption, tagged+always both-block-and-final delivery, partial suppression for tagged TTS on caption-capable channels, plain tagged block delivery, media block delivery with text stripped, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` gate: suppress ACP block delivery and defer text settlement; `canCaptionFinalTts` for tagged mode; `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` tracking |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.ts` | `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` state tracking + `hasDeliveredFinalTtsMedia()` accessor; narrow `suppressBlockUserDelivery` to text-only blocks (media blocks delivered with text stripped) |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts` | Regression tests: media block delivery with text stripped under `suppressBlockUserDelivery`, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts` | Regression tests: deferred settlement, block suppression, tagged streaming, tagged directive TTS, ACP live text deferral |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/acp-projector.ts` | `deferLiveTextUntilFinalFlush` option to suppress live text flushing for tagged TTS |
| `src/tts/directives.ts` | `resolveDirectiveOnlyTtsCaptionText` parser helper to extract clean caption from directive-only responses |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.ts` | `captionedFinalText: true` capability declaration |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts` | Test for capability declaration |
| `src/channels/plugins/types.core.ts` | JSDoc for `captionedFinalText` capability contract |
| `src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts` | Capability seam test |
| `docs/tools/tts.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability: opt-in criteria via `capabilities.tts.voice`, tagged mode behavior, text-only fallback, plugin API snippet |
| `docs/plugins/sdk-channel-plugins.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability in channel plugin SDK guide: opt-in declaration, media block preservation, fallback behavior, tagged mode |
| `docs/.generated/plugin-sdk-api-baseline.sha256` | Updated SDK API baseline hash |

## Tests

```
$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts

$ npx vitest run extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts

$ npx vitest run src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts

```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Telegram TTS final-mode text-before-voice churn on both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths, plus tagged mode partial preview leaking raw `[[tts:text]]` directives, plus media block suppression during captioned final TTS.

- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout at commit `05b4483a8f`, macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0. Live Telegram bot (`@thomas_fu_bot`) with Microsoft TTS (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`), `messages.tts.mode: "final"`.

- **Failing proof before fix (live Telegram)**:

  ![Before fix — separate text message + voice message (churn)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-before-fix.png)

  3. Tested with `messages.tts.auto: "always"` and `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"` — sent plain messages and directive-bearing messages to `@thomas_fu_bot` on Telegram

- **Evidence after fix**: Always mode (`messages.tts.auto: "always"`) at commit `05b4483a8f`:

  ![Always mode — voice with caption, single message](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-always-mode.png)

  Always-mode replies produce a single voice note with caption text. No text churn, no separate text bubble.

- **Evidence — Media block preservation with captioned final TTS at commit `05b4483a8f`**:

  ![Media block preserved — image delivered + voice note with caption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-media-block.png)

  When the bot generates an image during a TTS-enabled conversation (`auto: "always"`), the image is delivered immediately while text is deferred to the voice note caption. No media blocks are suppressed, and caption text does not duplicate as a separate text message.

- **Observed result after fix**: Always TTS auto mode delivers voice notes as single messages with caption text on Telegram. Media blocks (images, files) are preserved and delivered immediately with text stripped. No text flash, no duplicate messages, no media loss.

- **What was not tested**: Other TTS providers (only Microsoft TTS tested live). Group chat TTS (tested in DM only). Other channels with `captionedFinalText` capability (only Telegram tested). Tagged mode live proof pending — covered by unit tests (partial suppression + directive-only caption regression tests added).

## Settle-lifecycle reconciliation (rebased onto current main)

Current `main` made the delivered-transcript mirror fire-and-forget so reply completion no longer blocks on `dispatcher.waitForIdle()`. An earlier revision of this PR gated the captioned-final text fallback on an inline `await dispatcher.waitForIdle()` inside the reply operation, which would reintroduce exactly that completion-vs-idle block.

The fallback rides the same dispatcher settle lifecycle instead of an inline wait, and it is attributed **per captioned voice payload** rather than by aggregate dispatcher counters:

- Each captioned final (and its synthesized-voice sibling) is tagged with a unique capture token stored in the payload metadata, which survives the dispatcher's internal re-normalization.
- Before enqueue, a per-payload cancelled hook and a per-payload delivery-failed hook are registered, both keyed to that capture token. The delivery-failed hook (`appendReplyDispatcherBeforeDeliverFailed`) is a core-internal observer symmetric to the existing per-payload cancelled hook — it is not part of the plugin-facing dispatcher surface.
- A post-settlement task registered via `registerReplyDispatcherSettledTask` (the same seam the transcript mirror uses) runs after `waitForIdle()` inside `settleReplyDispatcher`, out of the reply hot path. It re-sends the accumulated block text as a text-only final **if and only if this specific captioned voice's own send was cancelled or failed** — never based on the aggregate final-outcome delta.

This matters because a single reply can enqueue multiple finals (a captioned voice plus sibling reasoning/commentary/status finals). The previous aggregate-count comparison mis-attributed a sibling final's failure or cancellation to the captioned voice, re-sending text the voice note had already delivered as its caption — reintroducing the exact churn this PR removes. Per-payload attribution fixes that: recovery follows the captioned voice's own outcome, mirroring the per-send attribution the ACP path already uses. A mixed-outcome regression asserts that a captioned voice which succeeds while a sibling final fails does **not** re-send the caption text. This preserves the churn fix and the async-failure text fallback while keeping reply completion off `waitForIdle`, so the fire-and-forget contract from the current transcript-mirror behavior is not regressed.

### Cancelled final delivery (not just failed)

A `beforeDeliver` / `reply_payload_sending` hook returning `null` **cancels** a send after `enqueue()` has already reported acceptance. That outcome is tracked as *cancelled*, not *failed* (`getCancelledCounts()` vs `getFailedCounts()` on the dispatcher). The ACP direct-visible-text settlement previously folded only failed counts into its undelivered accounting, so a cancelled captioned voice final left `finalMediaDelivered` set and skipped the deferred text fallback — silently dropping the reply text (the block text was already suppressed for the captioned path).

The settlement now folds cancelled block/final counts alongside failed counts (`settleDirectVisibleText` in `dispatch-acp-delivery.ts`, via a new `readDispatcherCancelledCounts` reader mirroring the failed reader). A cancelled captioned voice final therefore clears `finalMediaDelivered` and the deferred text fallback delivers the accumulated text. The non-ACP path now applies the same per-payload cancelled/failed attribution described above (a cancelled captioned voice recovers its text; a sibling's cancellation does not). A regression test drives an asynchronously cancelled captioned voice on Telegram and asserts the plain-text fallback fires.

Closes #83511

target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate — producing **invalid Unicode in the outbound API request**.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. The fix switches to `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, an existing repo helper.

## Outbound payload proof (real behavior)

Input: 41-code-unit tool call ID with 🐱 surrogate pair at positions 39-40.

### BEFORE fix (`id.slice(0, 40)`) — BROKEN

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\ud83d"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 40 code units, trailing **unpaired high surrogate** `\uD83D`
- Invalid Unicode sent to OpenAI API — downstream rejection risk

```
Output: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa�" (40 units)
Unpaired surrogate at tail: FAIL
```

### AFTER fix (`truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)`) — SAFE

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 39 code units, clean ASCII
- Valid Unicode sent to OpenAI API

```
Output: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" (39 units)
Unpaired surrogate at tail: none (PASS)
Length ≤ 40: PASS
```

**Evidence**: The `onPayload` hook intercepts the exact outbound JSON before `fetch` — the same bytes the OpenAI API receives. The captured payload above is the real API request content.

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` — `slice(0,40)` → `truncateUtf16Safe` |
| **Sibling UTF-16 PRs** | #104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839 — same helper |
| **Callers** | `convertMessages` → `streamOpenAICompletions` — cross-model tool-call path |
| **Test** | 47/47 pass; surrogate-pair boundary test with 41-unit 🐱 input |
| **Mutation proof** | Reverting to `slice` makes test FAIL: `trailing high surrogate: true` |
| **Payload proof** | Captured outbound JSON shows valid `tool_call_id` — no unpaired surrogate |
| **CI** | Rebased onto current `main` |

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider tool-call conversations produce valid Unicode in all IDs
- No change for IDs without surrogate pairs at the 40-unit boundary
- Non-OpenAI provider paths unchanged

target.title: fix(plugins): cleanup session scheduler jobs on failed registration rollback (#106825)
target.body:
Closes #106825

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a plugin that registers a session scheduler job and then throws during its `register` function would have its cleanup callback never invoked at the rollback boundary. The live session-scheduler record remained in module-global runtime state while the registry metadata was correctly restored — leaving external plugin-owned scheduler work (via `cleanup`) uncancelled after a failed registration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The registration rollback (`createPluginRegistrationTransaction`) restores the registry snapshot and calls `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` to clean up commands, interactive handlers, code-mode namespaces, context engines, and hooks — but did not clean up session scheduler jobs. These jobs are stored in two layers: a `registry.sessionSchedulerJobs` array (cleaned by the snapshot restore) and a separate module-global Map in `host-hook-runtime.ts` (previously never cleaned on rollback).

The fix adds the existing `cleanupPluginSessionSchedulerJobs` call to the `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` function in `registry.ts`, filtered to the rolling-back plugin's records. The cleanup is fire-and-forget (`void`) because the rollback lifecycle is synchronous while the cleanup callbacks may be async (external resource cancellation). Any cleanup failures are logged as warnings via `pushDiagnostic`.

## User Impact

Plugins that register session scheduler jobs with a `cleanup` callback will now have that callback invoked when their registration transaction is rolled back (e.g., a later exception during the same `register` function). No functional change for the common case where registration succeeds or where no session scheduler job is registered.

## Evidence

**Focused regression test** — `plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts` (3 tests, all passing):

```
 ✓ plugins src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts (3 tests) 82ms
```

**Real-behavior proof script** (standalone `tsx` harness exercising production code paths — `createPluginRegistry` → `createPluginRegistrationTransaction` → `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` → `cleanupPluginSessionSchedulerJobs`):

Before rollback: 1 live job, 1 registry entry
After rollback:
- cleanup callback calls: 1
- cleanup context: {"reason":"disable","sessionKey":"agent:main:main","jobId":"audit-job"}
- live jobs: [] (removed from module-global state)
- registry sessionSchedulerJobs: [] (restored by snapshot)

All three assertions pass: cleanup invoked once, live record removed, registry snapshot restored.

**Existing contract tests** — `scheduled-turns.contract.test.ts` (24 tests) and `run-context-lifecycle.contract.test.ts` (15 tests) both pass unaffected.

---

This PR is AI-assisted. Analysis, implementation, and testing were performed using opencode with review by the author.

target.title: fix(agents): greedily pack the code mode quick index so one oversized entry cannot blank it
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Code Mode quick index sorts declared-output tools first (#110317) and truncates to 8000 chars by keeping the longest contiguous **prefix** of lines that fits (binary search). If a single line alone exceeds the budget — a tool with a multi-KB id (`${source}:${owner}:${tool.name}`, where owner/name come from installed plugins and aren't length-capped) or a pathological input hint — the fitting prefix is 0 lines, so the **entire** quick index is blanked for that agent. A single buggy or hostile plugin thereby removes every declared-output contract hint, including core tools. Found via adversarial fuzzing during the stress pass that landed #110417; deferred from there.

## Why This Change Was Made

`formatCodeModeCatalogIndex` (`src/agents/code-mode.ts`) now greedily packs lines in the existing deterministic sorted order: it includes each line that keeps the rendered index within budget and **skips** any single line too large to fit, rather than dropping the whole tail after it. This:

- prevents one oversized entry from blanking the index (the reported failure mode);
- fits strictly more declared contracts when the declared tier alone overflows 8000 chars;
- is a simplification (removes the binary search).

Skipped entries stay fully discoverable through `ALL_TOOLS`, and packing over a deterministically sorted input keeps prompt bytes stable for provider prompt caches.

## User Impact

Code Mode agents on plugin-heavy or pathological catalogs keep their declared-output contract hints instead of losing the whole index to one bad entry. For existing catalogs whose index already exceeded 8000 chars, the packed content can differ slightly (a one-time prompt-cache miss); normal-sized catalogs render the full index unchanged.

## Evidence

- New regression: a declared tool with a ~9000-char id sorted first no longer blanks the index; all four short declared contracts survive and the oversized line is skipped (`src/agents/code-mode.test.ts`).
- New determinism test: same catalog produces a byte-identical truncated index across rebuilds.
- Full `src/agents/code-mode.test.ts`: 78 tests green.

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The saveCronQuarantineFile function archives overflowing quarantine sidecar files using timestamped unique filenames, but repeated overflow recovery can accumulate unlimited archive files on disk, causing unbounded disk growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper review flagged unbounded archive growth as a merge risk. Each overflow event creates a new archive file (quarantinePath + timestamp + random + ".archive.json"), and without a retention policy, repeated recovery cycles could exhaust disk space.

## What Changed

- Added CRON_QUARANTINE_ARCHIVE_MAX_COUNT = 5 constant
- Added listQuarantineArchives(): reads the directory, extracts timestamps from archive filenames, returns entries sorted oldest-first
- Added pruneOldQuarantineArchives(): when archive count exceeds 5, deletes the oldest archives
- archiveQuarantineFile() now calls pruneOldQuarantineArchives() after each archive creation
- Archive filenames use the shape: {quarantinePath}.{timestamp}.{random}.archive.json

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal operation. At most 5 archive files are retained on disk regardless of how many overflow recovery cycles occur. Old archives are deleted silently.

## Evidence

- Code: src/cron/store.ts lines 396-456 contain listQuarantineArchives and pruneOldQuarantineArchives
- Test: src/cron/store.test.ts line 375 - 'prunes oldest archives when the retention limit is exceeded' creates 7 overflow cycles and asserts at most 5 archives remain
- The test uses realistic oversized sidecar content to trigger actual archive creation and pruning
- Pattern: atomicWrite + rename preserves consistency; best-effort unlink avoids race conditions
- Unique filenames prevent collisions when multiple processes quarantine simultaneously

target.title: fix(scripts): bound sync-labels GitHub CLI operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `gh` CLI operations in the sync-labels script could hang indefinitely during GitHub API calls. When the GitHub API is unreachable or rate-limited, `execFileSync` calls to `gh api` and `gh label` would block without any timeout, stalling CI label synchronization workflows.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync` calls to external commands that touch the network must include a timeout and kill signal. Without these, transient API outages cause resource leaks and indefinite stalls. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation).

## User Impact

Label synchronization can complete or fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely when GitHub API endpoints are unresponsive.

## Evidence

- The change adds a `SYNC_LABELS_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to both `execFileSync("gh", ??` call sites.
- Pattern consistency: matches the bounding approach in `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325).

target.title: fix(memory-embeddings): use longer backoff for rate-limit (429) errors
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `openclaw memory index` encounters a rate-limit (429 / RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED) error from the embedding provider, the retry loop uses the normal 500ms base delay with an 8000ms cap. Rate-limit windows are typically 60 seconds, so all 3 retries exhaust in under 5 seconds and the entire index operation fails. The reporter's log shows retries completing at `~553ms/526ms/520ms/548ms/1028ms/1194ms` — nowhere near the 60s window required.

## Changes

- **New `isRateLimitMemoryEmbeddingError()` in policy** — two-part classifier requires BOTH a status indicator (429 / too many requests / RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED / resource has been exhausted) AND a rate-limit keyword, so pure quota/billing messages (which won't recover in 60s) fall through to the normal short retry path
- **`rateLimitBaseDelayMs` (30s) param on `runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop`** — when a rate-limit error fires, use this base instead of the normal `500ms`; produces wait sequence: 30s → 60s → 120s
- **`rateLimitMaxAttempts` param** — separate attempt budget for rate-limit errors so they don't burn through the normal retry budget
- **Explicit `isRateLimitMemoryEmbeddingError(err)` in `waitForEmbeddingRetry`** — replaced the fragile delayMs heuristic with an explicit predicate check on the actual error
- **Threaded through `runMemoryEmbeddingBatchRetryWithSplit`** — both retry loops and recursive split calls get the same longer backoff for rate-limit errors
- Normal transient errors (connection reset, fetch failed, timed out, 5xx) still use the original 500ms base — no regression

## Evidence

- All 19 tests pass (17 original + 2 new for Google-style RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED)
- Test `uses longer backoff for rate-limit errors` confirms: 429 with default config produces waits = [30000, 60000] before exhausting 3 attempts
- Test `uses longer backoff for Google-style RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED with rate-limit keyword` confirms the canonical provider throttle spelling gets the same long backoff
- Test `still uses short backoff for non-rate-limit retryable errors` confirms: transient `fetch failed` with the same config still uses [500ms] delay — no cross-contamination
- Test for quota RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED confirms: pure billing messages are not retried (not classified as retryable) — no spurious 60s waits for quota exhaustion
- The `waitForEmbeddingRetry` max-delay now uses explicit `isRateLimitMemoryEmbeddingError(err)` instead of the old delayMs heuristic

target.title: feat: allow standalone MCP Apps to use bound tools and resources
target.body:
Closes #110451

## What Problem This Solves

Standalone MCP App links could render an App but could not use its owning server's App-visible tools or resources. Apps that work in the authenticated Control UI therefore lost their interactive behavior when opened through the ticketed standalone host.

## Why This Change Was Made

The standalone host now exposes a closed, typed MCP tool/resource bridge backed by the same view-bound authorization and operation layer as the authenticated Control UI. It keeps the process-local ticket threat model: every privileged request revalidates the ticket, runtime session, live view, server ownership, App visibility, allowlist, read-only state, rate/concurrency limits, and runtime lease.

The browser bridge advertises `serverTools` and `serverResources` only after their handlers are installed, validates the official MCP request schemas on the server, binds postMessage traffic to the validated dedicated sandbox origin, and never accepts or forwards general Gateway RPC or operator credentials.

## User Impact

Fresh ticketed standalone MCP App views can now call their allowed App-visible tools and read owning-server resources. Transcript-reconstructed views remain tool-read-only. Existing authenticated Control UI behavior remains on the same operation contract and ordinary model tools are unchanged.

This PR is independently deployable. It adds no config key, environment variable, protocol-version bump, compatibility shim, plugin, channel UI, approvals UI, or public-host behavior.

## Evidence

- Fresh autoreview after simplification: clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- Focused Gateway proof: 18 tests passed across `mcp-app-standalone.test.ts` and `server-methods/mcp-app.test.ts`.
- Real Chromium conformance: official ext-apps initialization completed; an App-only tool and owning-server resource succeeded; a model-only call was rejected; reload within the lease succeeded; tampering and live lease revocation failed closed.
- Security assertions prove standalone requests use only `MCP-App v1...`, never the Gateway bearer token, and the ticket is absent from HTTP URLs, referrers, and browser diagnostics.
- Type proof: `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:ui`, and `tsgo:core:test` passed.
- Static proof: targeted oxfmt and oxlint passed.
- Production proof: `pnpm build` passed; `npm pack --dry-run --json --ignore-scripts` produced `openclaw-2026.7.2.tgz` (112,449,491 bytes unpacked on the proved base).

Known gaps are intentional non-goals: no channel launch UI, portable actions, Telegram behavior, public-host configuration, approvals UI, or additional optional MCP capabilities.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound credential payload reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Lab credential add commands enforced `OPENCLAW_QA_CREDENTIAL_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` with a file stat before reading the payload. A payload file could grow after that stat and before the read, which let the command read and parse data beyond the configured cap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The credential payload reader now opens the file, verifies the opened handle is a regular file, and reads at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes from that handle. That keeps boundary-sized payload JSON accepted while rejecting files that are oversized at stat time or grow past the cap before the read, without reading the whole grown file into memory.

## User Impact

Operators using QA Lab credential pools get the configured payload byte limit applied to the actual bytes consumed by the CLI. Oversized or racing payload files fail before any credential broker request is sent.

## Evidence

- Current head: `7ff257fb1484a66925de3a2ef1f8c44a59a2389e`.
- Docker Linux proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.test.ts -- -t "credential payload"` passed in `node:24-bullseye`; the targeted file reported 4 passing tests and 101 skipped.

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` in `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` to prevent prototype pollution when changed config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` function in `src/config/mutate.ts:634` checks whether a changed top-level config key exists in the new config before writing. The original check uses the `in` operator which traverses the prototype chain. If `getChangedTopLevelKeys` returns a key like `"toString"`, `!(key in nextConfig)` returns `false` (because `Object.prototype.toString` exists), causing the code to access `nextConfig[key]` and retrieve a prototype function instead of a config value.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/mutate.ts:634`, `!(key in nextConfig)` uses the `in` operator where `key` comes from `getChangedTopLevelKeys(base, next)` — a config diff function that includes own enumerable keys from both base and next config.

## Root Cause
- `getChangedTopLevelKeys` uses `Object.keys()` to collect keys from both config objects — `Object.keys()` returns own enumerable properties, so a config with `toString: "my-value"` would include `"toString"` in the changed keys
- The guard at line 634 then checks `key in nextConfig` — the `in` operator traverses the prototype chain
- If `nextConfig` does NOT have its own `"toString"` but the prototype does, `in` returns `true`, bypassing the null-return guard

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Also added**: `testing` namespace exposing `getChangedTopLevelKeys` for regression coverage
- **Consistent**: Aligns with the codebase-wide migration to `Object.hasOwn` (446+ call sites)
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503 and #108200

## User Impact
- **Before**: If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property, the guard would fail to block and the function would proceed with a prototype value
- **After**: The guard correctly detects absent own properties and returns null safely

## Evidence
- **Before**: `"toString" in {}` → `true` (prototype chain) → guard bypassed → `nextConfig["toString"]` returns `Object.prototype.toString` (function)
- **After**: `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` → `false` (own properties only) → guard correctly returns null
- Regression test: `getChangedTopLevelKeys` detects prototype-named keys and `Object.hasOwn` blocks them in nextConfig lookup

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log(key + ' in nextConfig:', key in nextConfig);
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !(key in nextConfig));
console.log('nextConfig[key] type:', typeof nextConfig[key]);
"
# toString in nextConfig: true
# guard passes (null return): false
# nextConfig[key] type: string
# FAIL: prototype collision bypassed guard
#   nextConfig['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString (function)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log('Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, \"' + key + '\"):', Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
"
# Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, "toString"): false
# guard passes (null return): true
# PASS: prototype collision correctly detected
#   guard returns null — safe early exit
```

### Regression test (exercises getChangedTopLevelKeys + Object.hasOwn)
```bash
$ npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  47 passed (47)
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts` — 47 passed (45 existing + 2 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression tests:
  - `getChangedTopLevelKeys detects changes on own keys including prototype-named keys`
  - `Object.hasOwn check prevents prototype collision in nextConfig lookup`

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw nodes camera snap` help text advertised global defaults for `--quality` (`0.9`) and `--delay-ms` (`2000` ms), but the implementation intentionally leaves those values undefined so that each node platform applies its own default. This mismatch caused the original report in #107941.

The platform-specific contracts are documented in `docs/nodes/camera.md`:

- iOS: `quality` default `0.9`, `delayMs` default `0`
- Android: `quality` default `0.95`
- macOS: `delayMs` default `2000`

Closes #107941.

## Why This Change Was Made

Instead of forcing one platform's defaults onto all platforms, this PR keeps the CLI behavior unchanged (omitted flags stay omitted) and updates the help text to make that clear. It also adds focused RPC-forwarding tests so the contract is protected: omitted values are not sent, and explicit values are forwarded verbatim.

## User Impact

No runtime behavior change for existing users. The help text now correctly describes platform-specific defaults, and the contract that the node owns the default values is covered by tests.

## Evidence

### Built CLI help output (after fix)

Captured from a local `tsdown` build of commit 786c657 with Node 24.15.0:

```
                              gateway.remote.url when configured)
```

### Focused test run


Result:


The test directly inspects the `camera.snap` `node.invoke` params passed to `callGatewayCli`, confirming omitted values are absent and explicit values are present.

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` in `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` to prevent prototype pollution when config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` function in `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75` iterates over source config entries and checks whether each key is absent from the runtime config. The check uses the `in` operator, which traverses the prototype chain. If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property name (e.g. `"toString"`, `"constructor"`), `!(key in runtime)` incorrectly returns `false`, causing the code to enter the recursive `else` branch and call `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(sourceValue, runtime[key])` where `runtime[key]` resolves to a prototype function.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75`, `!(key in runtime)` uses the `in` operator on a plain config object where `key` comes from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data.

## Root Cause
- The `in` operator traverses the prototype chain; `Object.hasOwn` checks only own properties
- Config keys come from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data
- The same function uses `Object.keys()` (own properties only) for iterating, creating an inconsistency
- The same file already has `Object.hasOwn(value, "$include")` at line 85 — this site was missed (path drift)

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Consistent**: The same file uses `Object.hasOwn` at line 85 for `"$include"` and at lines 41-42 in `createMergePatch`
- **Zero overhead**: Identical performance characteristics
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503

## User Impact
- **Before**: A config key named `toString` or `constructor` would bypass the "new key" check and enter recursive projection with a prototype function
- **After**: Prototype-named keys are correctly treated as absent from runtime and kept as-is

## Evidence
- **Before**: `!("toString" in {})` returns `false` (prototype pollution causes wrong branch)
- **After**: `!Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` returns `true` (correct — treated as new key)
- Regression test added: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
// With '!(key in runtime)': 'toString' in {} → true (prototype)
// Goes to else branch with runtime['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString
console.log('FAIL: typeof result.toString:', typeof result.toString);
"
# typeof result.toString: function (should be string)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
console.log('PASS: result.toString:', result.toString);
"
# result.toString: my-value
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/io.write-prepare.test.ts` — 54 tests passed (53 existing + 1 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression test: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

target.title: fix(signal): preserve reverse-proxy path prefixes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running the native Signal channel behind a reverse proxy path prefix, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8080/signal`, would still send RPC, health-check, and SSE requests to the origin root (`/api/v1/...`) instead of the configured prefix (`/signal/api/v1/...`).

That can make Signal send/check/receive flows fail with 404s even though `channels.signal.httpUrl` points at the correct mounted Signal service.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveSignalEndpointUrl` now keeps the parsed base URL pathname before appending the Signal native endpoint suffix. Root-mounted base URLs keep the existing `/api/v1/...` behavior, while path-prefixed base URLs now resolve beneath the configured prefix.

The change is limited to the native Signal client URL join helper. Container-mode Signal URL construction is separate and already preserves its configured path prefix, so it is intentionally unchanged.

## User Impact

Operators can run the native Signal HTTP/SSE API behind a path-prefixed reverse proxy and use the same configured `httpUrl` for sends, health checks, and event streaming.

## Evidence

### Live reverse-proxy behavior proof

I ran the current PR head against a local path-prefixed reverse-proxy setup:

```text
OpenClaw Signal native client
-> http://127.0.0.1:<proxy-port>/signal
-> path-prefixed reverse proxy
-> native-compatible signal-cli JSON-RPC/SSE service
```

This proof does not use a private Signal account or credentials. It validates the deployment behavior changed by this PR: the native OpenClaw Signal client preserves the configured `httpUrl` pathname before sending RPC, health-check, and SSE requests.

```text
[proof topology] OpenClaw Signal native client -> path-prefixed reverse proxy -> native-compatible signal-cli JSON-RPC/SSE service
[proof baseUrl] http://127.0.0.1:63713/signal
[before-current-main-shape] new URL('/api/v1/check', baseUrl).pathname=/api/v1/check -> HTTP 404
[openclaw] signalCheck(baseUrl) -> ok=true status=204
[openclaw] signalRpcRequest('version') -> {version:proof-signal-native}
[openclaw] streamSignalEvents(account=<redacted-e164>) -> [{event:message,data:{"source":"reverse-proxy-proof"},id:proof-1}]
[proxy] GET /api/v1/check rejected outside /signal mount -> 404
[proxy] GET /signal/api/v1/check -> 204
[proxy] POST /signal/api/v1/rpc -> 200
[proxy] GET /signal/api/v1/events?account=<redacted-e164> -> 200
[mock-native-signal] GET /api/v1/check -> 204
[mock-native-signal] POST /api/v1/rpc method=version -> 200
[mock-native-signal] GET /api/v1/events?account=<redacted-e164> accept=text/event-stream -> 200
```

### Focused tests

Focused behavior covered in tests:

- RPC request: `http://server/signal/` resolves to `/signal/api/v1/rpc`.
- Health check: `http://server/signal` resolves to `/signal/api/v1/check`.
- SSE receive stream: `http://server/signal` resolves to `/signal/api/v1/events?account=...`.
